name: Caesar
description: Canada's briny brunch guardian: vodka and clam-tomato juice under a celery-salt crown. Sounds alarming, converts skeptics daily.
funFact: Walter Chell invented it in Calgary in 1969, drawing inspiration from spaghetti alle vongole; Canadians now drink hundreds of millions of Caesars a year.

name: Greyhound
description: A lean, quick two-parter of spirit and grapefruit juice. Tart, refreshing, and faster out of the gate than its bus-terminal pedigree suggests.
funFact: Add a salted rim and it becomes a different dog entirely — the Salty Dog; the Greyhound name is tied to the Post House restaurants at Greyhound bus terminals.

name: Brandy Alexander
description: Cognac, dark crème de cacao, and cream dusted with nutmeg — a chocolate truffle you can drink. Deceptively gentle for something brandy-based.
funFact: It was John Lennon's drink of choice during his 1970s 'Lost Weekend' in Los Angeles — he reportedly likened it to a milkshake.

name: Espresso Martini
description: Cold, bittersweet, and crowned with dense crema foam — a nightcap and a wake-up call occupying the same glass. Contains no vermouth and makes no apology.
funFact: Dick Bradsell created it at London's Soho Brasserie in 1983 for a customer who asked for something that would wake her up, then mess her up; he first called it the Vodka Espresso.

name: Grasshopper
description: Green crème de menthe, white crème de cacao, and cream shaken into mint-chocolate velvet. A supper-club survivor the color of its namesake insect.
funFact: It is credited to Philibert Guichet of New Orleans' Tujague's restaurant, who reputedly entered it in a 1919 New York cocktail competition and took second place.

name: Porto Flip
description: Port, brandy, and a whole egg yolk shaken into custard and dusted with nutmeg. The last commonly cited survivor of the once-mighty flip family.
funFact: Early American flips were heated by plunging a red-hot fireplace poker straight into a tankard of ale, rum, and egg, making the drink hiss and froth.

name: White Russian
description: Vodka and coffee liqueur smothered in cream — dessert wearing a bathrobe. It ties no room together better than a bowling alley bar.
funFact: It languished in obscurity until 'The Big Lebowski' (1998), whose bathrobe-clad hero The Dude drinks little else for the entire film.

name: Gin Fizz
description: A gin sour shaken hard and topped with soda, meant to be drunk quickly while the sparkle lasts. Once a standard morning restorative, an idea best left in its century.
funFact: The fizz family entered print in the 1876 edition of Jerry Thomas's bartending guide and became a turn-of-the-century American morning institution.

name: Ramos Gin Fizz
description: Gin, citrus, cream, egg white, and orange flower water shaken into a trembling white column that rises above the rim. As much a feat of endurance as a beverage.
funFact: Demand at Henry Ramos's New Orleans bar was so fierce that he employed a relay of 'shaker boys' — reportedly around 35 during the 1915 Mardi Gras, and they still couldn't keep up.

name: Bushwacker
description: The Gulf Coast's boozy milkshake apex predator: rum, coffee, chocolate, and coconut whirred into soft-serve with a hidden bite.
funFact: It was born at a St. Thomas beach bar in 1975 and adopted by Pensacola's Sandshaker Lounge in 1980, which turned it into a Florida Panhandle institution.

name: Frozen Margarita
description: A Margarita passed through a blizzard until it becomes wearable weather. Salt rim, straw, instant vacation.
funFact: In 1971, Dallas restaurateur Mariano Martinez converted a soft-serve ice-cream machine into the world's first frozen margarita machine — it now sits in the Smithsonian.

name: Miami Vice
description: A frozen odd couple sharing one glass: strawberry daiquiri on one side, piña colada on the other. Crockett and Tubbs in slush form.
funFact: Ordering one means the bar makes you two complete frozen cocktails and pours them side by side; the name nods to the pastel-drenched 1980s TV series.

name: Americano
description: Campari and sweet vermouth stretched with soda — the Negroni's gentler ancestor. Bitter enough to feel adult, light enough to have two.
funFact: It is the very first drink James Bond orders in the very first novel, 'Casino Royale' (1953) — before the Vesper was ever invented.

name: Bloody Mary
description: A savory meal masquerading as a drink: vodka, tomato juice, and a spice rack's worth of seasoning. The only cocktail routinely garnished with breakfast.
funFact: Fernand Petiot claimed to have first mixed it at Harry's New York Bar in 1920s Paris; when he brought it to New York's St. Regis hotel, it was primly renamed the Red Snapper.

name: Cape Codder
description: Vodka wading through cranberry juice like a bog farmer at harvest. Tart, rosy, and dressed with a lime wedge for the tourists.
funFact: Cranberry cooperative Ocean Spray first printed the vodka-cranberry recipe in 1945 under the considerably less relaxing name 'Red Devil.'

name: Cuba Libre
description: Rum and cola with a firm squeeze of lime — the lime being the entire legal difference between this and an ordinary rum and Coke.
funFact: Its name — 'Free Cuba' — was the rallying cry of Cuban independence, and the drink spread after Coca-Cola arrived in Havana with American forces following the Spanish-American War.

name: Dark 'n' Stormy
description: Inky dark rum brooding over spicy ginger beer like a squall over open water. Bermuda's unofficial national drink, with the paperwork to prove its seriousness.
funFact: Gosling Brothers trademarked the name, so in the United States a drink legally sold as a Dark 'n Stormy must be made with Gosling's Black Seal rum.

name: El Diablo
description: A devil in a ginger-beer disguise. Blackcurrant liqueur gives tequila a wicked purple grin beneath the fizz.
funFact: It appeared in Trader Vic's 1946 book as the "Mexican El Diablo," making it one of the earliest tequila cocktails in print.

name: Fernet con Coca
description: Argentina's national handshake: brutally bitter Italian amaro tamed by sweet cola. Locals call the foamy pour an art form; newcomers call for water.
funFact: Argentines are so devoted to the combination — affectionately nicknamed the "Fernandito" — that Argentina consumes more than three-quarters of the world's fernet.

name: Gin and Tonic
description: A crisp colonial artifact of gin, quinine tonic, and lime that turned medicine into an institution. Under UV light, the quinine in the glass glows faintly blue.
funFact: British officers in 19th-century India mixed gin into their daily antimalarial quinine ration to make the bitter medicine palatable.

name: Gin Rickey
description: The driest of the classic highballs: gin, a whole lime's worth of juice, and soda with no sugar at all. Washington's swamp-summer survival kit, still in service.
funFact: It is named for lobbyist 'Colonel Joe' Rickey, whose original 1880s version at Washington's Shoomaker's bar used bourbon; in 2011 the D.C. Council declared the Rickey the capital's official native cocktail.

name: Long Island Iced Tea
description: Vodka, gin, rum, tequila, and triple sec conspiring under a splash of cola to impersonate iced tea. Famous for being far stronger than it tastes.
funFact: Despite the name it contains no tea; bartender Robert 'Rosebud' Butt claimed he invented it for a 1972 cocktail contest at Long Island's Oak Beach Inn.

name: Mojito
description: Havana's garden in a glass: rum lengthened with soda over bruised mint, lime, and sugar. Beloved by drinkers, quietly dreaded by bartenders in a rush.
funFact: Its supposed ancestor, a rough aguardiente remedy called 'El Draque,' is said to be named after the English privateer Sir Francis Drake.

name: Moscow Mule
description: Vodka, ginger beer, and lime served in a frosty copper mug that does half the work. Neither from Moscow nor mule-powered, but unstoppable since 1941.
funFact: It was engineered at Hollywood's Cock 'n' Bull pub in 1941 to move two slow sellers at once: Smirnoff vodka and the house-brand ginger beer.

name: Paloma
description: Tequila lengthened with grapefruit soda and lime over a salted rim — brighter, thirstier work than its margarita cousin.
funFact: In Mexico the Paloma — 'dove' in Spanish — is widely considered the country's most popular tequila cocktail, outdrinking the margarita on its home turf.

name: Pimm's Cup
description: An ambulatory English garden: cucumber, mint, and fruit bobbing in gin-based Pimm's and lemonade. Standard-issue equipment at lawn tennis.
funFact: It began in the 1840s as a digestive "house cup" served in tankards at James Pimm's London oyster bar; today tens of thousands of pints pour at Wimbledon every year.

name: Ranch Water
description: West Texas hydration protocol: tequila, lime, and aggressively bubbly mineral water. Tastes like dusk on a caliche road.
funFact: Texas lore says ranchers made it by drinking an inch off a bottle of Topo Chico and topping it up with tequila and lime, straight from the bottle.

name: Screwdriver
description: Vodka and orange juice, full stop. The cocktail equivalent of a firm handshake: simple, direct, and done in seconds.
funFact: Legend credits American oil workers abroad who stirred vodka into orange juice with an actual screwdriver; the name was already appearing in Time magazine by 1949.

name: Sea Breeze
description: Vodka refreshed with cranberry and grapefruit, tasting exactly like its name suggests. A staple of sunburned patios everywhere.
funFact: An earlier 1920s drink of the same name mixed gin and grenadine — the vodka-cranberry version only took over decades later during the great cranberry-juice marketing boom.

name: Seven and Seven
description: Blended whiskey and lemon-lime soda in permanent disco formation. Two ingredients, one number, zero pretension.
funFact: Tony Manero orders 7&7s at the disco in Saturday Night Fever (1977), sealing the drink's status as official fuel of the polyester era.

name: Tequila Sunrise
description: Tequila and orange juice with grenadine sinking into a layered dawn. More sunrise aesthetics than mixological rigor, and perfectly content with that.
funFact: The modern version was created at the Trident bar in Sausalito in the early 1970s and went global after Mick Jagger discovered it at a 1972 Rolling Stones tour party.

name: Tinto de Verano
description: Spain's low-effort summer survival fluid: red wine lengthened with lemon soda over ice. Cheerfully unpretentious and served by the pitcher.
funFact: The name means "summer red wine," and many Spaniards order it over sangria, which they regard as a drink for tourists.

name: Tom Collins
description: Effectively gin lemonade with bubbles, served tall and unhurried. A drink so easygoing it was once the punchline to a national prank.
funFact: In the Great Tom Collins Hoax of 1874, Americans told friends that a man named Tom Collins was slandering them in a nearby bar, sending victims off to hunt a man who did not exist.

name: Whisky Highball
description: Whisky, ice, and soda water — a drink so minimal it becomes a meditation. Japan elevated its construction into near-ceremonial craft.
funFact: In Japan the highball became so beloved that Suntory sells it ready-made in cans at convenience stores nationwide.

name: Hot Toddy
description: Whiskey, honey, lemon, and hot water — equal parts cocktail and folk remedy. Prescribed by grandmothers far more often than by doctors.
funFact: The word 'toddy' likely derives from tari, a fermented palm-sap drink British colonists encountered in India, long before Scotland claimed the hot version.

name: Irish Coffee
description: Hot coffee, Irish whiskey, and sugar drunk through a floating lid of lightly whipped cream. Weather protection disguised as dessert.
funFact: Chef Joe Sheridan invented it in the 1940s to thaw weary transatlantic flying-boat passengers at Foynes; San Francisco's Buena Vista Cafe imported the recipe in 1952 and now serves thousands a day.

name: Mint Julep
description: Bourbon poured over a mountain of crushed ice and fresh mint until the silver cup wears a coat of frost. The American South's answer to air conditioning.
funFact: It has been the official drink of the Kentucky Derby since 1938, with nearly 120,000 juleps served at Churchill Downs each Derby weekend.

name: Sherry Cobbler
description: Sherry, sugar, and fresh fruit heaped over crushed ice — the drink that taught 19th-century America to love ice, straws, and afternoon drinking.
funFact: The most fashionable American drink of the 19th century, it is credited with popularizing the drinking straw — Charles Dickens's 'Martin Chuzzlewit' features a character marveling over one.

name: Benton's Old Fashioned
description: Breakfast and nightcap fused into one specimen. Bacon-fat-washed bourbon meets maple syrup, smelling faintly of a diner griddle in the best possible way.
funFact: Don Lee's 2007 creation at PDT popularized the fat-washing technique and is named for Benton's, the Tennessee smokehouse that supplies the bacon.

name: Bramble
description: A gin sour caught in a berry thicket. Blackberry liqueur bleeds down through crushed ice like juice through a hedgerow after rain.
funFact: Dick Bradsell created it in 1984, inspired by childhood memories of picking blackberries on the Isle of Wight.

name: Breakfast Martini
description: Toast and marmalade dissolved into gin. A spoonful of orange preserves gives this citrusy specimen its charmingly sticky disposition.
funFact: Salvatore Calabrese invented it in 1996 after his wife insisted he actually eat breakfast — he brought the marmalade to work instead.

name: Chartreuse Swizzle
description: An alpine liqueur gone tropical, swizzled through crushed ice with pineapple and spice. Green, glacial, and quietly potent.
funFact: Marcovaldo Dionysos built the drink for a 2003 Chartreuse competition around a 110-proof liqueur whose full 130-herb recipe is known only to Carthusian monks.

name: Division Bell
description: A smoky toll from the mezcal belfry. Aperol and maraschino ring bright over the char, announcing last call in the prettiest way possible.
funFact: Phil Ward invented it in 2009 at his agave-obsessed New York bar Mayahuel and named it after the Pink Floyd album The Division Bell.

name: Eastside
description: A gin sour that took up gardening. Cucumber and mint keep everything cool and shaded, like drinking the far corner of a greenhouse.
funFact: It descends from the Southside, the minted gin sour beloved in Prohibition-era speakeasies — the cooling cucumber is the modern upgrade.

name: Final Ward
description: The Last Word's rye-slinging descendant: equal parts, zero compromise. Herbal, sour, and strong enough to end arguments.
funFact: The name is a double pun by creator Phil Ward: his 'final' riff on the classic Last Word, with his own surname smuggled in.

name: French Martini
description: A silky relic of the '90s 'tini boom, foaming pale pink from a hard shake. Contains no vermouth and only one French passport holder.
funFact: Despite the name it was born in 1980s New York — the only French thing in it is Chambord, a raspberry liqueur from the Loire Valley.

name: Garibaldi
description: Two ingredients standing at attention: bitter red Campari beneath a cloud of 'fluffy' aerated orange juice. Breakfast-adjacent and proudly Italian.
funFact: It is named for unification hero Giuseppe Garibaldi because it marries northern Italy's Campari with the oranges of the south.

name: Gin Basil Smash
description: A garden brawl in a glass. Fistfuls of muddled basil turn gin and lemon a vivid chlorophyll green, smelling like summer and tasting like victory.
funFact: Jörg Meyer invented it at Hamburg's Le Lion in 2008 and initially called it the Gin Pesto; cocktail blogs spread it around the world within a year.

name: Gin-Gin Mule
description: A diplomatic summit between the Mojito and the Moscow Mule, chaired by gin. Ginger beer provides the fireworks; mint signs the accords.
funFact: Audrey Saunders designed it around 2000 as a gateway drink to convert vodka drinkers to gin, and it became her Pegu Club's calling card.

name: Gold Rush
description: Prospector's treasure in liquid form: bourbon panned through honey and lemon until only the nuggets remain. Simple, gleaming, and dangerously repeatable.
funFact: T.J. Siegal created it at Milk & Honey in 2001 by swapping honey syrup into a whiskey sour, using the honey mix the bar kept for its Bee's Knees.

name: Kentucky Buck
description: A bourbon buck with strawberry stains on its boots. Ginger beer kicks, fruit soothes, and the whole ride tastes like summer in the bluegrass.
funFact: Erick Castro created it at San Francisco's Rickhouse around 2010, and it became one of the most reprinted modern recipes in the ginger-spiked 'buck' family.

name: Naked and Famous
description: A smoky equal-parts hybrid that shows all its cards at once. Mezcal growls, Chartreuse hums, and Aperol keeps the whole confession bright.
funFact: Creator Joaquín Simó of Death & Co described it as the bastard love child of the Last Word and the Paper Plane, born in the mountains of Oaxaca.

name: Oaxaca Old Fashioned
description: An agave-speaking cousin of the bourbon original. Tequila carries the melody, mezcal supplies the campfire, and a flamed orange twist lights the way.
funFact: Phil Ward's 2007 Death & Co creation is widely credited with helping kick off the American mezcal boom.

name: Old Cuban
description: A Mojito that came into money. Aged rum and mint get dressed up with Champagne, trading the beach for a hotel ballroom.
funFact: Audrey Saunders, who later founded New York's influential Pegu Club, invented it in the early 2000s as a bridge between the Mojito and the French 75.

name: Porn Star Martini
description: A flamboyant passion fruit showpiece that arrives with its own entourage: a chilled shot of sparkling wine served on the side, for sipping between scenes.
funFact: Douglas Ankrah created it in 2002, and it has repeatedly ranked as the United Kingdom's most-ordered cocktail.

name: Red Hook
description: A Manhattan that moved across the river and got tougher. Punt e Mes brings the bitterness, maraschino whispers dark cherry down by the docks.
funFact: Vincenzo Errico created it at Milk & Honey in 2003, sparking a whole borough of Brooklyn-neighborhood riffs like the Greenpoint and the Bensonhurst.

name: Tommy's Margarita
description: A Margarita stripped to its agave soul: no orange liqueur, just tequila, lime, and nectar from the same plant that made the spirit. Purists nod; the plant approves.
funFact: Julio Bermejo created it at his family's Tommy's Mexican Restaurant in San Francisco in the early 1990s, and the IBA later added it to its official cocktail list.

name: Trinidad Sour
description: A rule-breaker that uses bitters as the base spirit rather than the seasoning. Orgeat and lemon tame a full pour of Angostura into crimson velvet.
funFact: Giuseppe González's 2009 recipe calls for a staggering ounce and a half of Angostura bitters — more than most bars use in a week of dashes.

name: White Negroni
description: A pale doppelgänger of Italy's famous bitter, rebuilt from French parts. Gentian root supplies the bite while Lillet smooths the edges to ivory.
funFact: British bartender Wayne Collins improvised it at a Bordeaux wine fair in 2001 when he couldn't find Campari and sweet vermouth, so he grabbed Suze and Lillet instead.

name: Dirty Shirley
description: A Shirley Temple that came of age and ordered vodka. Grenadine-sweet nostalgia with a fake ID.
funFact: The New York Times crowned it the 'drink of the summer' in 2022, decades after the mocktail it corrupts was named for child star Shirley Temple.

name: Jell-O Shot
description: A wobbling gelatin lifeform that carries liquor in structural form. Consumed by the tray, respected by no one, beloved by all.
funFact: Satirist Tom Lehrer claimed to have pioneered it in the 1950s to sneak liquor onto an Army base where drinks were banned at the Christmas party.

name: Fish House Punch
description: Jamaican rum, cognac, and peach brandy loosened with lemon and sugar in a communal bowl. Colonial America's most storied — and most underestimated — punch.
funFact: It was born in 1732 at Philadelphia's Schuylkill Fishing Company, a colonial angling club, and legend blames a conspicuously blank stretch in George Washington's diary on an encounter with it.

name: Sangria
description: Red wine steeped with chopped fruit, sweetener, and often a shot of brandy, served by the pitcher. Spain's most sociable export after the siesta.
funFact: Named for 'sangre' — Spanish for blood — it conquered the United States at the Spanish Pavilion of the 1964 New York World's Fair.

name: Batanga
description: Tequila and cola with a salted rim, stirred — by decree of its late inventor — with a well-worn kitchen knife. Humble ingredients, sacred technique.
funFact: Don Javier Delgado Corona invented it in 1961 at La Capilla in the town of Tequila and stirred every Batanga with the same knife he used to cut limes, tending his bar into his nineties.

name: Cantarito
description: Tequila and a citrus grove sharing a rustic clay cup. The vessel sweats, the drink stays cool, and Jalisco road trips suddenly make sense.
funFact: It is named for the little porous clay cup it's served in, which chills the drink through evaporation — devotees insist the cup drinks better with years of use.

name: Carajillo
description: Espresso fortified for active duty. On its Mexican tour it drafts vanilla-citrus Licor 43, foaming over ice into a caffeinated nightcap.
funFact: Folk etymology traces the name to 'coraje' — courage — from Spanish soldiers in colonial Cuba who spiked their coffee before duty.

name: Coquito
description: Puerto Rico's coconut Christmas elixir, thick as a lullaby and spiced with cinnamon. Appears in December, vanishes by Three Kings Day.
funFact: The name means "little coconut," and Puerto Rican families guard their recipes so fiercely that coquito tasting contests are a holiday institution.

name: Kalimotxo
description: Equal parts red wine and cola — the Basque Country's shrug at wine snobbery. Somehow far more than the sum of its cheap, brilliant parts.
funFact: As the story goes, it was christened at a 1972 Basque port festival when vendors rescued a batch of off wine by cutting it with Coca-Cola.

name: Michelada
description: Beer that went to battle and came back seasoned: lime, hot sauce, and a salted rim turn a lager into brunchtime armor.
funFact: One popular origin story credits Michel Ésper, a regular at a San Luis Potosí sports club, whose custom beer-and-lime order became "Michel-ada" — Michel's lemonade.

name: Queen's Park Swizzle
description: A Trinidadian tower of crushed ice, demerara rum, and mint, capped by a rust-red stratum of Angostura. Requires a swizzle stick and forearm commitment.
funFact: Born at Port of Spain's Queen's Park Hotel in the 1920s, it was praised by Trader Vic as "the most delightful form of anesthesia given out today."

name: Sgroppino
description: A Venetian slush of lemon sorbet whipped with prosecco and vodka. Half dessert, half palate cleanser, entirely committed to elegance.
funFact: Its name comes from Venetian dialect for untying a little knot — it was traditionally served between courses to loosen the palate at Venetian banquets.

name: Terremoto
description: Chile's 'earthquake': sweet young pipeño wine capped with a scoop of pineapple ice cream. The ground feels perfectly stable until you stand up.
funFact: Santiago lore says foreign journalists covering the 1985 earthquake named it for its ground-shifting effects — and a second round is called a réplica, an aftershock.

name: Ti' Punch
description: Martinique's minimalist ritual: grassy rhum agricole, a coin of lime, and a slick of cane syrup. No ice unless you ask, no apologies either way.
funFact: Caribbean custom dictates "chacun prépare sa propre mort" — each prepares his own death — so the bartender hands you the bottle and you mix your own.

name: Appletini
description: A neon-green Jolly Rancher of a drink from the height of the 'tini era. Tastes of sour apple candy; contains no measurable apple.
funFact: It debuted at Lola's in West Hollywood in 1997 as the "Adam's Apple Martini," named for the bartender who created it.

name: Fuzzy Navel
description: Peach schnapps and orange juice in unapologetic harmony. Soft, sweet, and named after a pun rather than a body part, honest.
funFact: The name is a double pun — fuzzy for the peach, navel for the orange — and the drink helped make 1980s peach schnapps one of the fastest-selling new liquors in US history.

name: Harvey Wallbanger
description: A Screwdriver crowned with a golden float of herbal Galliano. Its groovy name and cartoon mascot did most of the heavy lifting in the 1970s.
funFact: A 1970s Galliano marketing campaign built the drink around a sandal-wearing cartoon surfer whose slogan was "Harvey Wallbanger is the name. And I can be made!"

name: Midori Sour
description: A radioactive-green melon sour beamed straight from a 1980s dance floor. Sweet, kitschy, and completely unashamed of either.
funFact: Midori means 'green' in Japanese, and Suntory launched the liqueur in America with a 1978 party at Studio 54.

name: Mudslide
description: A milkshake that took a wrong turn into the liquor cabinet. Vodka, coffee liqueur, and Irish cream engulf everything in delicious sediment.
funFact: It was reportedly invented in the 1970s at the Wreck Bar at Rum Point on Grand Cayman, where it remains the house specialty.

name: Rusty Nail
description: Scotch sweetened by Drambuie's honeyed herbs, sipped slowly in leather-chair lighting. The official nightcap of ring-a-ding-ding.
funFact: Drambuie, its defining half, is tied to a legend that Bonnie Prince Charlie gave the secret recipe to the MacKinnon clan after the failed 1745 Jacobite rising.

name: B-52
description: A three-layer stratigraphy of coffee liqueur, Irish cream, and orange liqueur. Drink it fast or set the top alight; geology was never this festive.
funFact: A popular origin story credits Alberta bartender Peter Fich, who named his layered creations after favorite bands — this one for the B-52s.

name: Baby Guinness
description: A trompe-l'oeil shooter: coffee liqueur topped with a float of Irish cream so it resembles a miniature pint of stout, foam collar and all.
funFact: Despite the name and the perfect two-tone pour, it contains no Guinness at all.

name: Buttery Nipple
description: A dessert-counter shooter of butterscotch schnapps under a cool cream float. Zero sophistication, one hundred percent compliance.
funFact: The layering is pure physics: sugar-dense butterscotch schnapps sinks while the lighter Irish cream floats serenely on top.

name: Green Tea Shot
description: Irish whiskey and peach schnapps masquerading as a health beverage. Named purely for its jade hue — no leaves were steeped in its making.
funFact: It contains no tea whatsoever — the name comes entirely from the drink's pale green color.

name: Jägerbomb
description: A depth charge of German herbal liqueur plunged into an energy drink. The splash is part of the ceremony; the regret is complimentary.
glassware: Shot glass dropped in a pint glass
funFact: Jägermeister means "master hunter," and the glowing stag on its label honors St. Hubertus, the patron saint of hunters.

name: Kamikaze
description: Vodka, orange liqueur, and lime in equal thirds — a citrus dive-bomb with no survivors expected. Clean, sharp, and gone in one motion.
funFact: Add a splash of cranberry, serve it up in a stemmed glass, and the 1970s Kamikaze becomes the blueprint of the Cosmopolitan.

name: Lemon Drop
description: Vodka-lemonade compressed into candy form, with a sugared rim as the wrapper. Puckers first, forgives quickly.
funFact: It was created in the 1970s at Henry Africa's in San Francisco, widely described as America's first "fern bar."

name: Mind Eraser
description: A stratified vodka-and-coffee contraption drained through a straw from the bottom up. Does exactly what the label promises.
funFact: House rules require draining it in one continuous pull from the bottom — coffee liqueur first, fizzy water last — making it a carbonated Black Russian in a hurry.

name: Pickleback
description: A whiskey shot immediately chased by cold pickle brine, which erases the burn like it never happened. Chemistry-adjacent magic in two small glasses.
funFact: Bartender Reggie Cunningham poured the first one at Brooklyn's Bushwick Country Club in 2006, using brine from a jar of McClure's pickles stored at the bar.

name: Vegas Bomb
description: A whisky-peach-cranberry payload dropped into an energy drink. Detonates on contact with bachelor parties.
glassware: Shot glass dropped in a pint glass
funFact: Skip the energy-drink plunge and the shot inside goes by its own poker-table name: the Royal Flush.

name: Washington Apple
description: An orchard compressed into a shot glass: whisky, sour apple, and cranberry doing a crisp autumn impression all year round.
funFact: It salutes Washington State, grower of most of America's apples — yet its traditional whisky is Canadian.

name: Amaretto Sour
description: Almond liqueur brightened with lemon into something between marzipan and lemonade. Long dismissed as a starter drink, lately rebuilt with respect.
funFact: Bartender Jeffrey Morgenthaler famously declared in 2012 that he makes the world's best Amaretto Sour by adding cask-proof bourbon and egg white — a spec many bars now follow.

name: Aviation
description: Gin, maraschino, lemon, and a whisper of crème de violette tinting the glass the pale gray-blue of a cloudy sky. Delicate, floral, and easy to overdo.
funFact: Crème de violette vanished from the American market for decades, so generations of bartenders made colorless Aviations until imports resumed in 2007.

name: Bee's Knees
description: Gin, honey, and lemon — a Prohibition-era formula in which the honey did double duty as flavor and camouflage. Named with era-appropriate slang for 'the best.'
funFact: During Prohibition, honey and lemon conveniently masked the harsh bite of bathtub gin; one popular attribution credits Frank Meier of the Ritz Paris with the recipe.

name: Blood and Sand
description: Scotch, cherry liqueur, sweet vermouth, and orange juice in improbable equal-parts harmony — one of the only classics brave enough to mix Scotch with juice.
funFact: It was named after the 1922 Rudolph Valentino bullfighting film 'Blood and Sand' and preserved for posterity in the 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book.

name: Brandy Crusta
description: Cognac, curaçao, maraschino, and lemon dressed in a full sugared crust and an extravagant ribbon of lemon peel. The peacock ancestor of the Sidecar.
funFact: Joseph Santini's 1850s New Orleans creation is credited with introducing elaborate citrus garnish to the cocktail — the entire glass rim is 'crusted' in sugar.

name: Caipirinha
description: Cachaça muddled with whole lime and sugar in the glass it is served in. Brazil's national cocktail: rustic by design, lethal by volume.
funFact: One popular legend traces it to a São Paulo folk remedy for the Spanish flu made with lime, garlic, and honey — over time the garlic left and the cachaça stayed.

name: Clover Club
description: Gin, raspberry, lemon, and egg white shaken into a rosy cloud. Pretty in pink but pre-Prohibition to the bone.
funFact: It was named for a Philadelphia club of lawyers, writers, and industrialists who met at the Bellevue-Stratford Hotel from the 1880s onward — hardly the crowd its color suggests.

name: Corpse Reviver No. 2
description: Gin, Cointreau, Lillet, and lemon over an absinthe rinse — a member of the Victorian family of hangover 'cures' and comfortably the best of them.
funFact: Harry Craddock's 1930 'Savoy Cocktail Book' warns that 'four of these taken in swift succession will unrevive the corpse again.'

name: Cosmopolitan
description: A blush-pink shard of the 1990s: citrus vodka, cranberry, lime, and orange liqueur served up with maximum poise. Dismissed as a fad, it simply never left.
funFact: Its origin is disputed among several American bartenders, but nobody disputes what made it a global icon: Carrie Bradshaw ordering round after round on 'Sex and the City.'

name: Daiquiri
description: Rum, lime, and sugar shaken to a snowy chill — nothing more is needed and nothing less will do. Often mistaken for its frozen, blended descendants.
funFact: It takes its name from Daiquirí, a beach and village near Santiago de Cuba, where American mining engineer Jennings Cox is credited with mixing it around 1898.

name: Gimlet
description: Gin and lime cordial, sharp and to the point — named, fittingly, after a small boring tool. A naval ration that retired ashore and never left.
funFact: Rose's lime cordial, patented in 1867, preserved lime juice without alcohol for the Royal Navy — the same lime rations that earned British sailors the nickname 'limeys.'

name: Hemingway Daiquiri
description: A bone-dry daiquiri sharpened with grapefruit and maraschino, built to a novelist's exacting and immodest specifications. Also answers to 'Papa Doble.'
funFact: Ernest Hemingway, wary of sugar, asked Havana's El Floridita for his daiquiri with no sugar and double rum — the resulting 'Papa Doble' was named in his honor.

name: Jack Rose
description: Applejack, grenadine, and citrus in a blushing pre-Prohibition sour. Orchard fruit with a literary pedigree and a slightly shady name.
funFact: Jake Barnes drinks a Jack Rose in a Paris hotel bar in Ernest Hemingway's 'The Sun Also Rises' (1926).

name: Last Word
description: Equal parts gin, Green Chartreuse, maraschino, and lime — an improbable herbal truce that tastes inevitable. Extinct for decades, now everywhere that matters.
funFact: Born at the Detroit Athletic Club around Prohibition, it was forgotten until Seattle bartender Murray Stenson unearthed it from a 1951 recipe book in 2004 and set off a global revival.

name: Lemon Drop
description: Citrus vodka, lemon, and sugar shaken into hard-candy form and served up with a sugared rim. Sweet, sour, and unashamed of either.
funFact: It was created in the 1970s at Henry Africa's in San Francisco, one of the original 'fern bars' that pioneered dating-friendly, plant-filled saloons.

name: Margarita
description: Tequila sharpened with lime and orange liqueur behind a crust of salt. A perennial contender for the most-ordered cocktail in the United States.
funFact: 'Margarita' is Spanish for 'daisy,' and the drink is structurally a tequila Daisy — a 19th-century sour template of spirit, citrus, and liqueur.

name: Paper Plane
description: Equal parts bourbon, Aperol, Amaro Nonino, and lemon folded into perfect bittersweet symmetry. One of the few 21st-century drinks already treated as canon.
funFact: Sam Ross devised it in 2008 for Chicago's The Violet Hour and named it after M.I.A.'s song 'Paper Planes,' which was playing on repeat at the time.

name: Penicillin
description: Blended Scotch with lemon and honey-ginger syrup under a smoky float of Islay malt. Medicine-cabinet branding, world-class execution.
funFact: Sam Ross created it at New York's Milk & Honey in 2005, and it spread to bar menus worldwide purely by word of mouth — the definitive modern classic.

name: Pisco Sour
description: Grape brandy, lime, and sugar under a snowdrift of egg-white foam dotted with bitters. The subject of a genial but eternal custody dispute between Peru and Chile.
funFact: Credited to American expat bartender Victor Morris in 1920s Lima, it is honored in Peru with a national Pisco Sour Day on the first Saturday of February.

name: Sidecar
description: Cognac, orange liqueur, and lemon balanced on a sugared rim — the sour family in evening wear. A relic of 1920s Paris that never went out of style.
funFact: It is supposedly named for an army captain who was chauffeured to his Paris bar of choice in a motorcycle sidecar.

name: Ward 8
description: A rye sour rounded with orange and grenadine — Boston machine politics rendered in liquid form, right down to the premature victory lap.
funFact: Legend says it was mixed at Boston's Locke-Ober in 1898 to toast Martin Lomasney's election win in the Eighth Ward — the night before the votes were actually counted.

name: Whiskey Sour
description: The archetype of the sour family: whiskey, lemon, and sugar in perfect three-point balance, optionally cushioned with a cloud of egg-white foam.
funFact: Its best-known variations earned names of their own: shaken with egg white it is often called a Boston Sour, and a float of dry red wine on top turns it into a New York Sour.

name: Aperol Spritz
description: A sunset-orange aperitivo of Aperol, prosecco, and soda built for golden-hour piazzas. Bitterness with training wheels, in the best possible way.
funFact: The spritz traces back to 19th-century Austrian soldiers stationed in the Veneto, who asked for local wine 'gespritzt' — splashed — with water to tame it.

name: Bellini
description: White peach puree lifted by prosecco into a pale-pink Venetian daydream. Insists on white peaches; yellow ones are considered a diplomatic incident.
funFact: Giuseppe Cipriani of Harry's Bar named it in 1948 because its pink glow reminded him of robes in paintings by the Renaissance master Giovanni Bellini.

name: Champagne Cocktail
description: A bitters-soaked sugar cube dissolving at the bottom of a flute of champagne, releasing a slow ribbon of spiced bubbles. Victorian glamour, still operational.
funFact: It appears in Jerry Thomas's 1862 guide and later earned Hollywood immortality — Victor Laszlo pointedly orders champagne cocktails in 'Casablanca.'

name: Death in the Afternoon
description: Absinthe clouding into iced champagne like slow opaline weather. Named after a book about bullfighting by the man who invented it, which explains a lot.
funFact: Ernest Hemingway contributed the recipe to a 1935 celebrity cocktail book with the instruction to 'drink three to five of these slowly.'

name: French 75
description: Gin and lemon given a champagne afterburner. Elegant enough for a wedding, potent enough to be named after artillery.
funFact: It is named after the French 75mm field gun of World War I, whose recoil the drink's kick was said to resemble; Harry's New York Bar in Paris popularized it.

name: Mimosa
description: Champagne diluted with orange juice, or orange juice elevated by champagne, depending on your brunch philosophy. Named for a flower it happens to match in color.
funFact: It appeared at the Paris Ritz around 1925, four years after London's nearly identical Buck's Fizz — the main difference being that the Fizz pours more champagne.

name: Negroni Sbagliato
description: A Negroni in which the gin was 'mistakenly' replaced with prosecco — a happy accident promoted to permanent menu status.
funFact: Sbagliato means 'mistaken' — Bar Basso's Mirko Stocchetto grabbed sparkling wine instead of gin mid-Negroni in 1972, and a viral 2022 interview clip made his error a worldwide order.

name: Seelbach
description: Bourbon, Cointreau, a startling fourteen dashes of bitters, and champagne — a drink whose flavor is genuine even if its history was not.
funFact: Its celebrated 'lost 1917 recipe' was a hoax: in 2016 its true creator admitted he invented the drink at the Seelbach Hotel in 1995 and fabricated the vintage backstory.

name: Black Russian
description: The White Russian's darker, leaner elder: just vodka and coffee liqueur over ice. Two ingredients, zero small talk.
funFact: Bartender Gustave Tops created it at Brussels' Hotel Metropole in 1949 for Perle Mesta, the United States ambassador to Luxembourg.

name: Boulevardier
description: A Negroni that traded gin for bourbon and moved somewhere with worse weather. Richer, rounder, and built for autumn.
funFact: It appears in Harry MacElhone's 1927 book and is credited to Erskine Gwynne, an American expat who edited a Paris magazine called The Boulevardier.

name: Hanky Panky
description: Gin and sweet vermouth given a dark herbal jolt of Fernet-Branca. Proof that a few drops of the right bitter can rename an entire drink.
funFact: Ada 'Coley' Coleman, the Savoy's legendary head bartender, mixed it for actor Charles Hawtrey, who sipped it and declared, 'By Jove! That is the real hanky-panky!'

name: Manhattan
description: Rye and sweet vermouth in stately equilibrium, seasoned with aromatic bitters. The borough it is named for reinvents itself constantly; the drink refuses.
funFact: The famous tale that it debuted at a banquet hosted by Winston Churchill's mother is almost certainly false — she was in England, pregnant with Winston, at the time.

name: Martinez
description: Old Tom gin and sweet vermouth kissed with maraschino and bitters — the plush Victorian ancestor from which the Martini was ruthlessly streamlined.
funFact: Often called the missing link between the Manhattan and the Martini, it first appeared in print in 1884, and the town of Martinez, California claims it with a commemorative plaque.

name: Martini
description: An austere, glacial aperitif of gin and dry vermouth that rewards precision and punishes hesitation. Its ideal ratio has been argued about for over a century without resolution.
funFact: The Martini grew steadily drier through the 20th century — Winston Churchill reputedly said the only vermouth required was a glance at the bottle across the room.

name: Negroni
description: Equal parts gin, Campari, and sweet vermouth: bitter, scarlet, and entirely sure of itself. A slow sipper that gradually trains the palate to crave it.
funFact: Legend holds that in 1919 Count Camillo Negroni asked a Florence bartender to stiffen his usual Americano by swapping the soda water for gin.

name: Old Fashioned
description: The fossil record of American drinking: spirit, sugar, and bitters arranged much as they were two centuries ago. It has survived every fad by simply refusing to evolve.
funFact: In 2015 Louisville, Kentucky declared the Old Fashioned its official cocktail and now celebrates it every June with 'Old Fashioned Fortnight.'

name: Sazerac
description: Rye, sugar, and Peychaud's bitters swirled in an absinthe-rinsed glass, served without ice and without hurry. New Orleans in liquid form.
funFact: In 2008 the Louisiana legislature proclaimed the Sazerac the official cocktail of New Orleans — one of very few drinks with a statutory hometown.

name: Vesper
description: Gin and vodka sharing one glass with a measure of aromatized wine — a Martini with dual citizenship, invented on the page rather than behind a bar.
funFact: Ian Fleming invented it in 'Casino Royale' (1953), where Bond names it after Vesper Lynd; the original Kina Lillet was reformulated away in 1986, so a period-accurate Vesper is now impossible.

name: Vieux Carré
description: Rye, cognac, sweet vermouth, and Bénédictine with two kinds of bitters — a drink as layered as the French Quarter it is named for.
funFact: Walter Bergeron created it in the 1930s at what is now the Hotel Monteleone, whose Carousel Bar still slowly rotates its drinkers one full turn every fifteen minutes.

name: Hugo Spritz
description: The Aperol Spritz's alpine cousin, pale green and smelling of elderflower meadows. Mint leaves drift through the bubbles like leaves on a mountain stream.
funFact: Bartender Roland Gruber invented it in South Tyrol in 2005 using lemon balm syrup — elderflower took over later — and says he picked the name Hugo almost at random.

name: Kir Royale
description: Champagne blushing violet with a whisper of blackcurrant. An aperitif that dresses for the occasion even when there isn't one.
funFact: It is named for Félix Kir, the wine-loving priest, Resistance figure, and mayor of Dijon who served the still-wine version at civic receptions to promote local cassis.

name: Bahama Mama
description: A sunset-colored double-rum lounger that never wears a watch. Coconut and grenadine blur together like the last hour of a beach day.
funFact: Bahamian bartender Oswald "Slade" Greenslade claimed he invented it at the Nassau Beach Hotel in 1961, naming it after a calypso-era song.

name: Blue Hawaii
description: Swimming-pool blue and garnished like a parade float. Curaçao dyes a rum-and-pineapple sour the exact color of a Waikiki postcard.
funFact: Hilton Hawaiian Village bartender Harry Yee invented it in 1957 when a Bols sales rep challenged him to build a drink around blue curaçao — four years before the Elvis film.

name: Fog Cutter
description: A long tiki haymaker that throws rum, gin, AND brandy behind orgeat and citrus, with a sherry float as the parting shot. Visibility drops fast.
funFact: Trader Vic wrote of his own creation: 'Fog Cutter, hell. After two of these, you won't even see the stuff.'

name: Jungle Bird
description: The rare tiki species with a bitter streak. Campari's red plumage flashes through dark rum and pineapple, giving this bird its unmistakable call.
funFact: It was created in the 1970s as a welcome drink at the Kuala Lumpur Hilton's Aviary Bar, where it was originally served in a ceramic bird-shaped vessel.

name: Navy Grog
description: A three-rum broadside rigged with honey and grapefruit, famously sipped through a cone of shaved ice. Built for sailors; adopted by presidents.
funFact: Richard Nixon was reportedly a devotee of the Navy Grog at the Trader Vic's in Washington, D.C.

name: Rum Runner
description: A Florida Keys fruit smuggle of banana, blackberry, and rum. Sweet enough to hide its cargo until well past the checkpoint.
funFact: Lore at the Holiday Isle Tiki Bar says it was invented to burn through overstocked liqueurs before inventory, and named for Prohibition-era smugglers.

name: Saturn
description: The gin-powered outlier of the tiki solar system. Passion fruit and almond orbit a juniper core, ringed appropriately with a lemon spiral.
funFact: Filipino-American bartender J. "Popo" Galsini rode the Saturn to victory at the 1967 IBA World Cocktail Championship — a rare gin drink in a rum-dominated genre.

name: Scorpion Bowl
description: A communal volcano of rum, brandy, and orgeat meant for a table of allies. Long straws converge; individual dignity does not survive contact.
funFact: Trader Vic adapted it from a potent punch he encountered in Honolulu, and the classic garnish is a floating gardenia.

name: Suffering Bastard
description: A wartime hangover cure that mixes gin and brandy under a ginger-beer flag of truce. Gruff name, surprisingly gentle bedside manner.
funFact: Joe Scialom invented it at Cairo's Shepheard's Hotel in 1942, and gallons were reportedly sent to the front to fortify troops at El Alamein.

name: Three Dots and a Dash
description: A wartime victory toast in liquid Morse code. Honey, allspice, and aged rum signal triumph, garnished with three cherries and a pineapple dash.
funFact: Don the Beachcomber named it during World War II for the Morse code spelling of "V" — dot dot dot dash — for victory.

name: Hurricane
description: A crimson double-barrel of rum and passion fruit served in its namesake lamp-shaped glass. New Orleans' preferred method of losing an afternoon.
funFact: Pat O'Brien invented it in 1940s New Orleans to burn through surplus rum — distributors then forced bars to buy cases of it to obtain scarce whiskey — and named it for the hurricane-lamp glass.

name: Mai Tai
description: Aged rum, lime, orange curaçao, and almond-rich orgeat — tiki's crown jewel, endlessly imitated and routinely butchered with pineapple juice.
funFact: When Trader Vic served the first one to Tahitian friends in 1944, one reportedly exclaimed 'Maita'i roa a'e!' — roughly 'out of this world, the best' — naming the drink on the spot.

name: Painkiller
description: Dark rum, pineapple, orange, and coconut cream under a blizzard of fresh nutmeg. Prescription strength varies from two to four ounces of rum.
origin: Jost Van Dyke, British Virgin Islands
funFact: It was born at the Soggy Dollar Bar, which has no dock — patrons swim ashore and pay with wet bills — and Pusser's later trademarked the name for its own rum.

name: Piña Colada
description: Rum, coconut cream, and pineapple blended into a beach vacation with an umbrella in it. Subtlety was never the assignment.
funFact: Credited to bartender Ramón 'Monchito' Marrero at San Juan's Caribe Hilton in 1954, it has been the official national drink of Puerto Rico since 1978.

name: Sex on the Beach
description: Vodka, peach schnapps, orange, and cranberry — the 1980s distilled into a highball. Orders itself best when shouted over loud music.
funFact: For all its spring-break reputation, it holds an official place on the International Bartenders Association cocktail list.

name: Singapore Sling
description: A rosy gin sling elaborated with cherry liqueur, pineapple, and herbs until it became a national landmark. The recipe varies; the legend does not.
funFact: Ngiam Tong Boon created it around 1915 at the Raffles Hotel's Long Bar, where tossing peanut shells straight onto the floor is still encouraged.

name: Zombie
description: Three rums, citrus, falernum, and spice engineered into tiki's apex predator. Tastes like fruit punch, behaves like heavy machinery.
funFact: Its creator Donn Beach guarded the 1934 recipe with coded, unlabeled bottles his bartenders mixed blind, and he capped customers at two Zombies apiece.

name: American Amber Lager
description: A friendly, caramel-tinted lager that splits the difference between a light lager and a Vienna. The workhorse of American regional breweries.
funFact: The flagship of Yuengling — founded in 1829 and America's oldest operating brewery — is an amber lager of exactly this stripe.

name: Czech Dark Lager
description: Tmavé pivo: a dark Czech lager balancing caramel, cocoa, and a surprising Saaz snap. Prague locals know it as the beer worth queuing in a 500-year-old pub for.
funFact: Prague's U Fleků brewpub has brewed its famous dark lager on the same site since 1499, making it one of the oldest continuously operating brewpubs in the world.

name: Märzen
description: The amber 'March beer' brewed strong before summer and lagered in cold cellars until fall. In America it appears each autumn wearing an Oktoberfest costume.
funFact: A 1553 Bavarian decree banned brewing between late April and late September, so March batches were brewed stronger to survive the summer — hence the name.

name: Munich Dunkel
description: Bavaria's original brown lager, all bread crust and cocoa softness with none of the roastiness its color suggests. For centuries this, not helles, was simply what beer meant in Munich.
funFact: Dunkel was the default Bavarian lager for centuries — when the 1516 Reinheitsgebot purity law was written, the beer it protected looked like this.

name: Schwarzbier
description: The 'black pilsner' — a lager dark as ink yet startlingly light on its feet. It flashes roast and chocolate, then vanishes with a crisp lager snap.
funFact: Goethe was a devoted drinker of Köstritzer schwarzbier and is said to have lived on it during an illness when he could barely eat.

name: Vienna Lager
description: An amber lager with a gentle toasted-malt glow, invented in Vienna and then nearly forgotten there. It found a second life an ocean away in Mexico.
funFact: Anton Dreher created it in 1841, and after it faded in Austria the style survived mainly in Mexico, carried there by Central European immigrant brewers.

name: American Amber Ale
description: A copper-hued peacekeeper balancing caramel malt against citrusy American hops. One of the founding species of the craft brewing boom.
funFact: New Belgium's Fat Tire carried the amber banner for three decades until a controversial 2023 recipe overhaul made the beer lighter and crisper.

name: Irish Red Ale
description: A smooth, russet session ale with caramel sweetness and a dry, gently roasted tail. A quieter Irish icon that lives in the stout's long shadow.
funFact: The style's American fame owes much to Coors licensing 'George Killian's Irish Red' from Lett's Brewery of Enniscorthy, which had stopped brewing in 1956.

name: Barrel-Aged Barleywine
description: A barleywine matured in spirit barrels until it verges on liquid dessert: toffee, oak, and sherried fruit in slow motion. Hunted at festivals and cellar raids.
funFact: Like whiskey distillers, brewers lose part of every barrel to evaporation during aging—a tribute known as the angel's share.

name: Barrel-Aged Imperial Stout
description: An imperial stout that slumbered for months inside bourbon barrels, absorbing vanilla, oak, and whiskey fire. The crown jewel of many a bottle-share.
funFact: Goose Island's Bourbon County Stout, first brewed in the early 1990s in Jim Beam barrels, launched the entire barrel-aged stout phenomenon.

name: Belgian Blonde Ale
description: A golden, honeyed abbey ale with a gentle fruity-spicy shimmer from its Belgian yeast. The diplomatic entry point to the abbey beer family.
funFact: The style rose in the early 20th century as Belgian brewers crafted golden ales to win back drinkers defecting to pilsner.

name: Belgian Dubbel
description: A russet-brown abbey ale whose dark candi sugar conjures raisin, fig, and warm spice. Monastic in origin and meditative in effect.
funFact: The modern dubbel was codified at Westmalle Abbey in 1926, when the Trappist monks reformulated their brown beer for public sale.

name: Belgian Golden Strong Ale
description: A pale, effervescent trickster whose innocent straw color conceals devilish strength. Fruity, spicy, and dangerously easy to drink.
funFact: The archetype, Duvel, reportedly earned its name—Flemish for 'devil'—when an early taster declared the beer 'a real devil.'

name: Belgian Quadrupel
description: The heaviest evolution of the abbey line, dark as monastery oak and dense with fig, plum, and warming spice. Trappist brewers guard its greatest specimens.
funFact: The name 'Quadrupel' was coined in 1991 by the Dutch Trappist brewery La Trappe for its strongest beer, and the label stuck to the whole style.

name: Belgian Tripel
description: A deceptively golden abbey ale that hides formidable strength behind pear, spice, and a champagne-like sparkle. Handle with respect.
funFact: Westmalle brewed the golden strong beer that defined the style in 1934; devotees still call Westmalle Tripel 'the mother of all tripels.'

name: Bock
description: A strong, malty dark lager that originated in the northern town of Einbeck before Bavaria adopted it and never gave it back. Powerful but polite, like a large dog that thinks it's a lapdog.
funFact: Bavarians mispronounced 'Einbeck' as 'ein Bock' — a billy goat — which is why goats have been butting their way onto bock labels ever since.

name: Doppelbock
description: The monks' 'liquid bread' — a double-strength bock brewed rich enough to sustain a Lenten fast. Deep toffee and dark fruit with a velvet warmth that arrives like a heavy blanket.
funFact: Paulaner monks brewed the original, named Salvator, as nourishment during Lent — and imitators have honored it by ending their doppelbock names in '-ator' ever since.

name: Eisbock
description: A doppelbock concentrated by freezing: the ice is removed and everything intense stays behind. The rare apex predator of the lager family.
funFact: Legend credits a Kulmbach brewery apprentice who left a barrel of bock outside on a freezing night — the partially frozen 'accident' inside turned out to be delicious.

name: Maibock
description: The pale spring member of the bock family, tapped in May with more hop bite than its darker siblings. Sunshine in lager form, with a kick hidden in the gold.
funFact: Munich's Hofbräu traces its Maibock to 1614, and the ceremonial first keg is still tapped at the Hofbräuhaus each spring.

name: American Brown Ale
description: An English brown ale that emigrated and picked up a citrusy hop habit. Deeper roast and bolder bitterness distinguish it from its ancestor.
funFact: In 1980s homebrewing circles the hopped-up version was known as 'Texas brown ale' before the style earned its official name.

name: English Brown Ale
description: A nutty, amber-brown creature from England's northeast, malty but never heavy. Its caramel-toast character made it a working town's badge of pride.
funFact: Newcastle Brown Ale is nicknamed 'Dog' by locals, from the old excuse of 'going to walk the dog' as cover for a trip to the pub.

name: Dark Mild
description: A near-extinct, low-alcohol species once fed to England's factory workers by the pintful. Soft, dark, and gently sweet, it rewards those who track one down on cask.
funFact: The British campaign group CAMRA promotes May as 'Mild Month' in an ongoing effort to save the style from extinction.

name: English Bitter
description: The gentle heart of the British pub, low in strength and served nearly flat from the cask. Its name badly oversells its actual aggression.
funFact: Bitter and pale ale are historically the same beer—'bitter' is what drinkers called it at the bar, while 'pale ale' is what brewers printed on the bottle.

name: Extra Special Bitter
description: The strongest form of the bitter family, layering rich toffee malt over firm English hops. Abroad it became a style; at home it is essentially one famous beer.
funFact: In Britain 'ESB' is a Fuller's trademark for the beer it launched in 1971; only outside the UK did the name grow into a whole style.

name: Bière de Garde
description: The French farmhouse counterpart to saison, rounder and maltier, brewed to be 'kept' through the warm months. Often emerges from a corked bottle like sparkling wine.
funFact: The name means 'beer for keeping'—farm brewers made it in the cool seasons and cellared it, and many are still sold in corked champagne-style bottles.

name: Saison
description: A dry, peppery farmhouse ale once brewed to slake the thirst of summer field hands. Its wild-mannered yeast gives every specimen a slightly different personality.
funFact: Saisons were brewed in the cool months for seasonal farm workers called saisonniers, who reputedly received several liters a day as part of their wages.

name: Altbier
description: Düsseldorf's copper-colored answer to Cologne's Kölsch, its eternal rival: an old-style ale fermented cool for smooth, bitter-balanced clarity.
funFact: 'Alt' means 'old' in German, referring to the old top-fermenting method the city kept even after lager brewing conquered the rest of the country.

name: Cream Ale
description: A pale, ultra-smooth American hybrid that walks like a lager but ferments like an ale. Contains no cream whatsoever, despite persistent rumors.
funFact: Cream ale was pre-Prohibition America's ale-brewed answer to pilsner, often lightened with corn or rice to match the lager's crispness.

name: Kölsch
description: Cologne's delicate golden native: an ale fermented cool and lagered cold, yielding a crisp beer with a whisper of fruit. Served in small glasses that never stay empty for long.
funFact: Under the 1986 Kölsch Konvention only breweries in and around Cologne may use the name, and waiters keep replacing your 200ml stange until you put a coaster on top.

name: American IPA
description: The apex predator of the modern taproom, all citrus and resin with a firm bitter bite. Its many regional evolutions have colonized nearly every bar in America.
funFact: IPA is by far the best-selling craft beer style in the United States, accounting for roughly half of all craft beer dollar sales.

name: Belgian IPA
description: A hybrid creature born when spicy Belgian yeast met brash American hops. Its fruity, phenolic aura confuses IPA hunters and Belgian devotees alike.
funFact: Brasserie d'Achouffe's Houblon Chouffe, released in 2006, was among the first commercial beers to fuse a Belgian tripel base with IPA-level hopping.

name: Black IPA
description: A paradoxical dark-type IPA that smells like grapefruit but pours like midnight. Once a taproom staple, it has retreated to the endangered list.
funFact: Greg Noonan's Vermont Pub & Brewery poured a 'Blackwatch IPA' in the 1990s, long before the style's brief 2010s boom under the name Cascadian Dark Ale.

name: Brut IPA
description: A champagne-dry IPA that ferments away every trace of sugar, leaving only sparkle and hop perfume. Blazed brightly across taplists in 2018, then nearly vanished.
funFact: Kim Sturdavant of San Francisco's Social Kitchen & Brewery invented the style in 2017 using amyloglucosidase, an enzyme borrowed from mass-market lager brewing.

name: Cold IPA
description: A crisp, stripped-down IPA fermented with lager yeast and lightened with rice or corn. Built to deliver maximum hop flash with zero malt interference.
funFact: Kevin Davey of Portland's Wayfinder Beer is credited with creating the style, releasing the first beer labeled 'cold IPA' in 2018.

name: Double IPA
description: An overclocked IPA with hops and alcohol both cranked past reason. Deceptively drinkable for its strength, which is precisely the danger.
funFact: Vinnie Cilurzo brewed the first known commercial double IPA at Blind Pig Brewing in 1994, doubling the hops to mask flaws in old equipment.

name: English IPA
description: The ancestral form of all IPAs, earthier and more restrained than its American descendants. Its lineage traces to pale ales that survived the long sea voyage to India.
origin: London and Burton upon Trent, England
funFact: George Hodgson's Bow Brewery in London dominated the late-1700s beer trade to India, laying the groundwork for the style's legend.

name: Milkshake IPA
description: A dessert-adjacent mutation thickened with lactose and often fruit or vanilla. Divides trainers into devoted collectors and horrified traditionalists.
funFact: The style emerged from a 2015 collaboration between Pennsylvania's Tired Hands Brewing and Sweden's Omnipollo.

name: New England IPA
description: A hazy, juice-bomb variant that traded bitterness for pillowy softness and orange-juice opacity. Emerged from Vermont and rapidly displaced its clearer cousins.
funFact: The Alchemist's Heady Topper is widely credited as the style's prototype, and the Brewers Association added 'Juicy or Hazy IPA' as an official category in 2018.

name: Session IPA
description: A lightweight forme of the IPA bred for endurance rather than power. Delivers full hop aroma at an ABV that permits repeat encounters.
funFact: Founders All Day IPA popularized the style and its 15-pack became one of the best-selling craft beer packages in America.

name: Triple IPA
description: The final evolution of the hop-forward line, a syrupy titan north of ten percent. Encountered mostly at special releases, where it draws crowds of trainers.
funFact: Russian River's Pliny the Younger, released for just two weeks each February, has drawn multi-hour lines and beer tourists from around the world.

name: West Coast IPA
description: A crystal-clear, bone-dry evolution of the IPA that attacks with pine and grapefruit. Prized by purists for its aggressive bitterness and total lack of haze.
funFact: Russian River brewer Vinnie Cilurzo coined the term 'lupulin threshold shift' to describe hopheads' ever-growing tolerance for bitterness.

name: American Pale Ale
description: The friendly ambassador of craft beer, balancing biscuity malt against bright citrus hops. Often the first wild hop-creature a new drinker encounters.
funFact: Sierra Nevada Pale Ale, first brewed in Chico in 1980 with Cascade hops, essentially defined the style for American craft brewing.

name: Blonde Ale
description: A gentle, sun-colored species that hides in plain sight on nearly every taproom menu. Low bitterness and a soft malt sweetness make it approachable to all trainers.
funFact: Brewers affectionately call blonde ale a 'lawnmower beer'—a gateway style designed to lure lager drinkers into the craft world.

name: English Pale Ale
description: The dignified elder of the pale ale line, favoring toffee malt and earthy hops over flash. Evolves best at cellar temperature, where its fruity esters emerge.
funFact: Brewers worldwide still add gypsum to their water to mimic Burton's mineral-rich wells, a process known as 'Burtonisation.'

name: American Ice Lager
description: A mass-market lager chilled below freezing so ice crystals form and are removed, nudging the strength up. A gas-station descendant of the noble eisbock.
funFact: Labatt launched the first mass-market ice beer in 1993, setting off the short but fierce 'Ice Beer Wars' among North American mega-breweries.

name: American Lager
description: The most-encountered beer creature in North America, found in every stadium, cooler, and dive. Light, fizzy, and inoffensive by careful design.
funFact: Corn and rice entered the recipe in the 1800s because protein-heavy American six-row barley made hazy, heavy beer — the adjuncts lightened the body and clarified the glass.

name: American Light Lager
description: An American lager put through an even finer sieve — fewer calories, fewer carbs, and flavor dialed down to a whisper. Its natural habitat is the tailgate.
funFact: Biochemist Joseph Owades invented light beer in 1967 as Gablinger's Diet Beer; the recipe flopped, was given away, and eventually became Miller Lite.

name: Czech Pilsner
description: The golden original that every pale lager on Earth descends from. Soft Bohemian water and Saaz hops give it a rounded, almost buttery bitterness that has been imitated for nearly two centuries.
funFact: The first batch was brewed in 1842 by Josef Groll, a Bavarian brewer hired by the citizens of Plzeň — making the world's first golden lager a German-Czech collaboration.

name: Dortmunder Export
description: The lager that powered Germany's industrial heartland — slightly stronger and rounder than a pils, slightly drier than a helles. A beer engineered for people who worked hard and drank accordingly.
funFact: At its mid-20th-century peak, Dortmund brewed more beer than any other city in Germany, most of it drunk by the coal and steel workers of the Ruhr.

name: Festbier
description: The golden, deceptively strong lager actually served at modern Oktoberfest. It drinks like a helles that has been quietly working out.
funFact: This paler style displaced the darker märzen as the official Oktoberfest pour in the 1990s, and only six Munich breweries are permitted to serve beer at the festival.

name: German Pilsner
description: The Czech original's leaner, drier northern cousin. Crisper water and a sharper hop snap make it finish like a knife — clean, bitter, and gone.
funFact: Pils is by far Germany's best-selling beer style, accounting for roughly half of all beer sold in the country.

name: India Pale Lager
description: What happens when an IPA's hop bill is grafted onto a lager's clean, cold skeleton. All the aroma, none of the fruity yeast noise.
funFact: The IPL emerged from American craft brewing around the early 2010s, and brewers still argue over whether it is a true style or just a very good idea.

name: Italian Pilsner
description: A German pils that studied abroad and came back better dressed. Dry-hopping with noble German hops adds a floral perfume no traditional pils would dare.
funFact: The style traces to a single beer: Tipopils, first brewed in 1996 by Agostino Arioli at Birrificio Italiano near Como.

name: Japanese Rice Lager
description: A lager honed to a razor's edge with rice in the grist, prized for a bone-dry finish the Japanese call karakuchi. Its true power is making the next bite of food taste better.
funFact: Asahi Super Dry's 1987 launch triggered Japan's 'Dry Wars,' with every major brewery rushing out its own super-dry lager within a year.

name: Kellerbier
description: Lager in its natural, unpolished state — unfiltered, gently carbonated, and hazy like it just woke up. Best encountered in a Franconian beer garden under chestnut trees.
funFact: The name means 'cellar beer'; it is traditionally left ungespundet — unbunged — so excess carbonation escapes the barrel, giving it a signature gentle fizz.

name: Mexican Lager
description: A sun-adapted lager often brewed with flaked maize, born when Central European brewers set up shop in 19th-century Mexico. Frequently spotted wearing a lime wedge.
funFact: Mexico is the world's largest exporter of beer, shipping more abroad than any other country.

name: Munich Helles
description: Bavaria's gentle everyday lager, built to showcase malt rather than hops. It goes down so easily that a liter feels like a suggestion rather than a commitment.
funFact: Spaten released the first helles in 1894 as Munich's defensive answer to the wildly popular pilsners arriving from Bohemia.

name: Pre-Prohibition Lager
description: A ghost from before 1920: the fuller, hoppier corn lager Americans drank before Prohibition wiped the recipe books clean. Modern brewers resurrect it like brewing archaeology.
funFact: The style was reconstructed largely by homebrewers digging through pre-Prohibition brewing logs, which showed far more hops than any modern American lager uses.

name: Zoigl
description: A communal lager brewed in shared village brewhouses of the Upper Palatinate, then fermented and served in private homes on a rotating schedule. Less a beer style than a social institution.
funFact: A six-pointed Zoigl star hung outside a house signals that this week's batch is being poured there — a system still running in a handful of towns like Windischeschenbach and Neuhaus.

name: American Porter
description: A robust revival of London's lost workhorse beer, rebuilt with more roast and American hops. Sits between brown ale and stout on the darkness spectrum.
funFact: Anchor Porter, launched in 1972, helped resurrect the style in America decades after Prohibition had all but wiped it out.

name: Baltic Porter
description: A smooth, powerful porter that evolved around the cold Baltic Sea, where it adopted lager fermentation. Silky dark fruit and licorice with none of the rough edges.
funFact: Despite the name, most Baltic porters are technically lagers—local brewers copied strong English export porters but fermented them cold with lager yeast.

name: English Porter
description: The original dark beer of the industrial age, softer and more chocolatey than its stout descendants. Once the fuel of an entire laboring city.
funFact: The beer takes its name from the street and river porters of 1700s London who adopted it, and it is often called the world's first industrially brewed style.

name: Smoked Porter
description: A porter infused with the campfire aura of smoked malt. Encountered near barbecue and bonfires, it splits opinion like few other dark types.
funFact: Alaskan Brewing's influential Smoked Porter, first released in 1988, uses malt smoked over local alder wood—the same wood used for Alaskan salmon.

name: Scottish Ale
description: A malt-forward creature of the cold north, where hops were expensive imports and sweetness ruled. Sessionable, coppery, and quietly caramelized.
funFact: The traditional names 60/-, 70/-, and 80/- (shilling) come from the 19th-century wholesale price per cask, which rose with the beer's strength.

name: Wee Heavy
description: The Scottish ale's fully evolved form: a rich, warming malt bomb with notes of caramel and dark fruit. Small in serving size, heavy in every other respect.
funFact: Also called Scotch ale, it is traditionally served in a thistle-shaped glass modeled on Scotland's national flower.

name: American Wild Ale
description: The American school of funk: brewers deploying Brettanomyces, Lactobacillus, and barrels with scientific abandon. Each release is a small ecosystem with a label on it.
funFact: Despite the name, most American 'wild' ales are carefully inoculated with lab-grown wild yeast strains — true spontaneous fermentation remains the rare exception.

name: Berliner Weisse
description: Berlin's featherweight sour wheat beer, tart as lemonade and barely stronger than kombucha. Locals famously tame it with a shot of raspberry or woodruff syrup.
funFact: Napoleon's troops occupying Berlin in the early 1800s are said to have dubbed it 'the Champagne of the North.'

name: Catharina Sour
description: Brazil's signature sour: a light, quick-soured wheat beer flooded with fresh tropical fruit — passionfruit, guava, cajá. Sunshine engineered for 90-degree humidity.
funFact: Born in Santa Catarina state in the mid-2010s, it became one of the first Brazilian-born beer styles recognized in international style guidelines.

name: Faro
description: Lambic softened with candi sugar — the sweetened, sessionable form that once flowed as Brussels' everyday cheap beer. Now a rare sighting even in Belgium.
funFact: In 19th-century Brussels faro was the working class's daily drink, sometimes sweetened further at the table with sugar and a muddler.

name: Flanders Red Ale
description: A sour red beer aged for up to two years in enormous oak vats until it tastes more like wine than beer. Cherry, balsamic, and oak in an unusually elegant package.
funFact: Its long maturation in giant oak foeders and vinous character earned it the nickname 'the Burgundy of Belgium.'

name: Framboise
description: Raspberry lambic — perfumed, pink, and deceptively pretty for something born of wild fermentation. The friendliest ambassador the sour beer kingdom has ever sent out.
funFact: Raspberries joined the lambic tradition in the 20th century, well after cherries, and sweetened framboise became many drinkers' first-ever taste of wild beer.

name: Gose
description: A tart wheat beer seasoned with coriander and — improbably — salt. Nearly extinct by the late 20th century, it now thrives in craft taprooms like a rediscovered fossil species.
funFact: It is named after the river Gose in Goslar, and its salt and coriander survived the Reinheitsgebot purity law only because it was grandfathered in as a regional specialty.

name: Gueuze
description: A blend of young and old lambics refermented in the bottle until fiercely carbonated and complex. Sour, funky, and cellar-worthy — the blender's art in liquid form.
funFact: Its vigorous bottle-fermentation and cork-and-cage presentation earned it the nickname 'Brussels Champagne.'

name: Kettle Sour
description: The speedrun of sour brewing: wort is soured with Lactobacillus right in the kettle, then boiled clean and fermented normally. Tartness on a weekday timeline.
funFact: Kettle souring produces in a day or two the acidity that traditional lambic methods need one to three years to achieve — which is why taproom sours became suddenly ubiquitous in the 2010s.

name: Kriek
description: Lambic refermented on sour cherries, emerging ruby-red, tart, and faintly almondy from the pits. Fruit and funk locked in an elegant standoff.
funFact: Traditional versions use whole Schaarbeek sour cherries, pits and all — the pits contribute the style's subtle marzipan note.

name: Lambic
description: Belgium's wild-fermented ancestor beer: the cooling wort is left open overnight so the native microbes of the Zenne valley can claim it. No two barrels ever turn out quite alike.
funFact: Lambic is fermented spontaneously in shallow open coolships and traditionally brewed only in the cooler months, when the wild airborne yeast is at its friendliest.

name: Oud Bruin
description: East Flanders' 'old brown' — a malty sour aged long and warm, then blended young into old like a solera. Darker, rounder, and less oaky than its red cousin to the west.
funFact: Unlike Flanders red, oud bruin traditionally sours during long aging in steel or lined tanks rather than oak, and blenders marry old and young batches to hit the house balance.

name: Smoothie Sour
description: A kettle sour loaded with so much fruit purée it pours thick and opaque, often with lactose and vanilla riding along. Half beer, half dessert, entirely unsubtle.
funFact: Some smoothie sours contain so much fermentable fruit that breweries warn buyers to keep the cans cold — refermentation in the can has caused documented explosions and recalls.

name: California Common
description: A Gold Rush survivor: lager yeast fermented warm in shallow vessels because ice was a luxury San Francisco didn't have. Toasty, minty, and proudly neither ale nor lager.
funFact: The traditional name 'steam beer' is a trademark of Anchor Brewing, which is why every other brewery must call the style California common.

name: Grodziskie
description: Poland's ghostly pale smoked wheat beer — light as a feather, fiercely carbonated, and made entirely from oak-smoked wheat malt. A style that died in the 1990s and clawed its way back.
funFact: Its brilliant clarity and champagne-level carbonation earned it the nickname 'Polish Champagne' before the last historic brewery closed in the 1990s; revivalists have since resurrected it.

name: Malt Liquor
description: An American lager bulked up with sugary adjuncts for extra strength at minimum cost, traditionally sold in 40-ounce bottles. The brash, misunderstood cousin of the lager family.
funFact: Despite the name, malt liquor contains no distilled liquor at all — it is simply an American legal term for lagers brewed above ordinary strength.

name: Non-Alcoholic Lager
description: A lager with the alcohol carefully removed or never created, once a punchline and now a booming shelf category. The rare beer you can encounter before noon without judgment.
funFact: In Germany, non-alcoholic beer is marketed as an isotonic sports drink — Erdinger Alkoholfrei sponsors marathons and hands out cold ones at finish lines.

name: Radler
description: Half lager, half lemon soda, all refreshment. Germany's official beverage of people who still have things to do this afternoon.
funFact: Radler means 'cyclist' — innkeeper Franz Xaver Kugler is credited with inventing it in 1922 by stretching his dwindling beer supply with lemon soda for a horde of thirsty cyclists.

name: Rauchbier
description: Bamberg's smoked lager, brewed with malt dried over open beechwood fires. Tastes like a campfire learned excellent table manners.
funFact: Before modern kilns, virtually all malt was smoky — rauchbier is a living fossil, and Bamberg's Schlenkerla still smokes its own malt over beechwood logs.

name: Foreign Extra Stout
description: A robust export stout built to endure tropical shipping lanes, stronger and fruitier than the draught version. It found its truest home far from where it hatched.
funFact: Guinness Foreign Extra Stout descends from a 'West India Porter' first brewed in 1801, and Nigeria today buys more Guinness than Ireland does.

name: Imperial Stout
description: A colossal dark-type brewed strong enough to survive frozen sea voyages to the Russian court. Dense with espresso, dark chocolate, and warming strength.
funFact: The 'imperial' title comes from the style's popularity at the court of Catherine the Great, to which London brewers exported it in the 1700s.

name: Irish Dry Stout
description: A jet-black creature with a creamy white crown, roasty and surprisingly light on its feet. Its famous cascading pour is a nitrogen-powered special move.
funFact: The nitrogen pour that defines the modern pint was invented in 1959 by Michael Ash, a mathematician working for Guinness.

name: Milk Stout
description: A sweet stout fortified with lactose, the milk sugar that yeast cannot digest. The result is a rounder, creamier beast than its dry Irish cousin.
funFact: Britain banned the name 'milk stout' in 1946 over fears it misled the public into thinking the beer contained actual milk.

name: Oatmeal Stout
