description: A stout given a silken texture by a dose of oats in the mash. Smooth and gently roasty, like breakfast reimagined by a brewer.
funFact: The style was nearly extinct until 1980, when Samuel Smith's brewed one at the request of an American importer after beer writer Michael Jackson lamented its disappearance.

name: Oyster Stout
description: A briny curiosity sometimes brewed with real oysters or their shells, which lend a subtle mineral snap. Its bond with shellfish dates to the Victorian pub table.
funFact: Stout and oysters were a classic Victorian pairing, but the first brewery known to put actual oysters in the brew did so in New Zealand in 1929.

name: Pastry Stout
description: A dessert-mimic that disguises itself as cake, cookies, or pie using lactose, vanilla, and cacao. Sweetness levels can overwhelm unprepared trainers.
funFact: The term 'pastry stout' began as a half-insult on beer blogs in the late 2010s before brewers proudly adopted it as a badge.

name: American Barleywine
description: The English barleywine's brash cousin, layering a wall of citrus-pine hops over immense malt. Hibernates well, its bitterness mellowing into marmalade over years.
funFact: Anchor Brewing's Old Foghorn, first brewed in 1975, is regarded as the first modern American barleywine.

name: English Barleywine
description: A legendary sipping beast, dark with toffee and dried fruit, that improves for years in the cellar. Wine-strength, but unmistakably ale at heart.
funFact: Bass No. 1 is generally credited as the first beer marketed as a 'barley wine,' back in Victorian England.

name: Old Ale
description: An ancient English keeper-beer, aged until it develops dark fruit, leather, and a whisper of pleasant funk. A living fossil of pre-industrial brewing.
funFact: These beers were historically matured in wooden vats for months or years, and drinkers prized the aged character they called 'stale' as a compliment.

name: American Wheat Beer
description: A wheat beer run through a clean American filter: no banana, no clove, just soft grain and citrusy hops. The approachable gateway creature of many a craft taproom.
funFact: The style took off in 1980s Portland when Widmer Brothers brewed an American 'hefeweizen' with clean yeast — accidentally defining a new, banana-free category.

name: Dunkelweizen
description: A hefeweizen dressed in dark Munich malts, layering banana-bread and caramel over the familiar clove spice. Autumn's answer to the summer wheat beer.
funFact: Before modern malting made pale malt cheap, most Bavarian wheat beers were dark — the dunkelweizen is closer to the historical original than today's golden hefeweizen.

name: Hefeweizen
description: Bavaria's cloudy wheat beer, famous for smelling of banana and clove despite containing neither. The haze is yeast, the flavors are chemistry, and the pleasure is very real.
funFact: The banana and clove notes come entirely from the yeast — the compounds isoamyl acetate and 4-vinylguaiacol — with no fruit or spice anywhere near the kettle.

name: Kristallweizen
description: A hefeweizen filtered to crystal clarity, trading its yeasty haze for champagne-bright sparkle. The rarely-seen polished form of a normally cloudy species.
funFact: It is sometimes served with a slice of lemon in Germany — a practice wheat beer purists regard as an act of vandalism.

name: Weizenbock
description: A wheat beer fused with bock strength: banana and clove riding atop dark fruit and bready muscle. The evolved final form of the hefeweizen line.
funFact: Schneider Weisse invented the style in 1907 with Aventinus, created to give wheat beer drinkers an answer to Munich's doppelbocks.

name: Witbier
description: Belgium's spiced white wheat beer, hazy pale and perfumed with coriander and orange peel. It went extinct in the 1950s and was brought back from the dead by a milkman.
funFact: After the last witbier brewery closed in the 1950s, local milkman Pierre Celis revived the style in Hoegaarden in 1966, single-handedly rescuing it from extinction.

name: Ice Wine
description: A dessert wine pressed from grapes harvested while frozen solid on the vine, often in the dead of night. The ice stays behind in the press, leaving pure concentrated nectar.
funFact: Canadian regulations require grapes for icewine to be picked at minus eight degrees Celsius or colder, and Canada is now the world's largest producer.

name: Moscato d'Asti
description: A gently fizzy, grapey-sweet whisper of a wine from Piedmont, so low in alcohol it barely counts. Tastes like biting into a chilled muscat grape at peak ripeness.
funFact: At around 5.5% alcohol, Moscato d'Asti is one of the lightest wines in the world — Piedmontese winemakers historically drank it with lunch so they could keep working.

name: Sauternes
description: Bordeaux's liquid gold, made from grapes deliberately left to be shriveled by 'noble rot'. The fungus concentrates sugar and conjures flavors no healthy grape could manage.
funFact: The noble rot fungus, Botrytis cinerea, only works its magic under the region's precise rhythm of misty mornings followed by dry, sunny afternoons.

name: Tokaji Aszú
description: Hungary's amber royalty, blended from individually picked botrytized berries and once reserved for the courts of Europe. Sweetness measured in the old 'puttonyos' scale of berry baskets.
funFact: Louis XIV of France famously dubbed it 'Vinum Regum, Rex Vinorum' — the wine of kings, the king of wines.

name: Trockenbeerenauslese
description: The rarest tier of German wine: individually plucked, botrytis-shriveled berries yielding mere drops of intensely sweet juice. Produced only in vintages when nature cooperates perfectly.
funFact: The tongue-twisting name means 'dry berry select harvest' — pickers may pass through a vineyard many times to gather single raisined berries by hand.

name: Vin Santo
description: Tuscany's 'holy wine', made from grapes dried on mats for months and then aged for years in small sealed barrels tucked under attic roofs. Amber, nutty, and made for dunking biscotti.
funFact: The classic Tuscan ritual is to dip crunchy cantucci almond biscuits directly into a glass of Vin Santo at the end of a meal.

name: Commandaria
description: An amber dessert wine of sun-dried Xynisteri and Mavro grapes from the foothills of Cyprus, made in recognizably the same way for millennia. Encountering a bottle in the wild is a genuine event.
funFact: Commandaria is often cited as the world's oldest named wine still in production, taking its name from a medieval Crusader commandery on Cyprus.

name: Madeira
description: A wine deliberately cooked and oxidized on a volcanic Atlantic island until virtually indestructible. Bracing acidity keeps its caramel depths from ever feeling heavy.
funFact: Madeira's heat-and-oxygen upbringing makes bottles from the 18th century still drinkable, and America's Founding Fathers reportedly toasted independence with it in 1776.

name: Marsala
description: Sicily's amber fortified wine, ranging from bone dry aperitif to sticky dessert form. Most Americans first encounter it hiding in a pan of chicken.
funFact: English merchant John Woodhouse began fortifying and shipping Marsala in 1773 so it would survive the sea voyage to Britain, turning a local Sicilian wine into a global staple.

name: Ruby Port
description: The youngest and brightest of the Port family, bottled early to preserve its deep red color and primary fruit. An approachable gateway into fortified territory.
funFact: Port is fortified mid-fermentation with 77% grape spirit, which stuns the yeast and locks in the wine's natural sweetness.

name: Tawny Port
description: Port that traded youthful fruit for decades in wooden casks, slowly fading to amber and gaining nut and caramel powers. Serve slightly chilled for maximum effect.
funFact: The age statement on a tawny Port — 10, 20, 30, or 40 years — refers to the average age of the blend, not the youngest wine in the bottle.

name: Vintage Port
description: The final boss of fortified wine, made only from a single declared harvest and built to outlive its buyers. Requires decanting, patience, and ideally an heir.
funFact: Vintage Port is made only in exceptional years 'declared' by each house — roughly three per decade — and spends just two years in barrel before decades of bottle aging.

name: Barbera
description: Piedmont's everyday companion: dark-fruited, low in tannin, and crackling with acidity. While Nebbiolo poses for portraits, Barbera does the actual dinner-table work.
funFact: Barbera is the most planted red grape of Piedmont, pouring the wine locals actually drink while Nebbiolo gets the glory.

name: Cabernet Franc
description: The leafy, aromatic elder of the Bordeaux clan, lighter on its feet than its famous offspring. In the Loire it appears alone, all raspberry and pencil shavings.
funFact: Cabernet Franc is a parent of both Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, making it the quiet patriarch of the entire Bordeaux family.

name: Cabernet Sauvignon
description: The apex predator of red grapes, armored in tannin and dark cassis. It adapts to nearly every wine region on Earth and dominates steakhouse lists without mercy.
funFact: DNA profiling at UC Davis in 1996 revealed Cabernet Sauvignon is the offspring of a chance cross between Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc.

name: Carmenère
description: A Bordeaux ghost that vanished from Europe and resurfaced alive in Chile, where it now thrives. Dark fruit runs alongside a telltale streak of green peppercorn and paprika.
funFact: Believed lost to the 19th-century phylloxera plague, Carmenère was rediscovered in Chile in 1994, where it had been mistaken for Merlot for over a century.

name: Gamay
description: The bright, bouncy sprite of Beaujolais, best served with a slight chill and minimal ceremony. Low tannin and juicy red fruit make it dangerously gulpable.
funFact: In 1395, Duke Philip the Bold of Burgundy banned Gamay from his lands by decree, denouncing it as a 'very bad and disloyal plant.'

name: Grenache
description: A sun-worshipper that trades color for strength, ripening to heady alcohol while staying pale and perfumed. Frequently encountered in disguise inside famous southern blends.
funFact: Grenache is one of the most widely planted red grapes on Earth, yet it mostly toils anonymously as the backbone of blends like Châteauneuf-du-Pape and Priorat.

name: Malbec
description: Driven from France by frost and fashion, it evolved a triumphant second form at high altitude in Mendoza. Inky, violet-scented, and clearly built for grilled meat.
funFact: World Malbec Day is celebrated on April 17, commemorating the 1853 initiative that brought French vine cuttings — Malbec among them — to Argentina.

name: Merlot
description: The velvet diplomat of Bordeaux: plush, plummy, and quick to befriend newcomers. Often observed softening the sharp edges of its fiercer blending partners.
funFact: US Merlot sales slumped after the 2004 film Sideways, in which the protagonist loudly refuses to drink it — a dip economists dubbed the 'Sideways effect.'

name: Mourvèdre
description: A brooding, sun-loving beast that demands heat to ripen and repays it with dark fruit, leather, and a whiff of the wild. Rarely seen alone; usually lurking in blends.
funFact: Known as Monastrell in its native Spain and Mataro in Australia and California, it supplies the brooding 'M' in GSM blends.

name: Nebbiolo
description: Deceptively pale and brutally tannic, it lures the unwary with roses and tar before striking. Long cellaring is required to tame it.
funFact: Nebbiolo likely takes its name from 'nebbia,' the fog that blankets Piedmont's hills during its late-October harvest.

name: Nero d'Avola
description: Sicily's dark champion, forged in volcanic heat and Mediterranean sun. Ripe black cherry with a warm, faintly spicy finish.
funFact: Its name means 'black of Avola,' after a small town in southeastern Sicily, and it is the island's most planted red grape.

name: Petite Sirah
description: Nothing about this wine is petite except the berries. It stains glasses, teeth, and reputations with some of the darkest, most tannic juice in California.
funFact: Petite Sirah is the grape Durif, a 19th-century French cross of Syrah and Peloursin named for the botanist who propagated it.

name: Pinot Noir
description: A famously temperamental creature that sulks in the wrong climate and transcends in the right one. Thin-skinned in every sense, it rewards patient handlers with silk and perfume.
funFact: Pinot Noir is genetically unstable and mutates readily — Pinot Gris and Pinot Blanc are simply color mutations of the very same variety.

name: Pinotage
description: A laboratory-born hybrid unique to South Africa, smoky and mulberry-dark with a divisive reputation. Modern specimens have evolved well beyond their rustic ancestors.
funFact: Pinotage was created in 1925 when scientist Abraham Perold crossed Pinot Noir with Cinsaut, then locally called Hermitage — hence the portmanteau name.

name: Sangiovese
description: Tuscany's sour-cherry heartbeat, bristling with acidity and dusty tannin. It insists on being served with food, preferably something involving tomatoes.
funFact: The name is thought to derive from the Latin 'sanguis Jovis' — the blood of Jupiter.

name: Syrah / Shiraz
description: A shape-shifter with two known forms: peppery and savage on Rhône granite, sunny and jam-packed as Australian Shiraz. Its signature move is a crack of black pepper behind dark fruit.
funFact: DNA testing in 1998 proved Syrah is a cross of two obscure French alpine grapes, Dureza and Mondeuse Blanche, debunking legends tying it to the Persian city of Shiraz.

name: Tannat
description: The name warns you: this is tannin incarnate, a black-fruited bruiser from France's rugged southwest. It found a gentler second home across the Atlantic in Uruguay.
funFact: Tannat contains some of the highest levels of tannins and procyanidins measured in any red wine grape, and Uruguay has adopted it as its national grape.

name: Tempranillo
description: Spain's noble workhorse, equally at home napping for years in oak barrels or bottled young and juicy. Leather and dried fruit emerge as it matures.
funFact: Its name comes from the Spanish 'temprano,' meaning early, because the grape ripens weeks ahead of most of its Iberian neighbors.

name: Touriga Nacional
description: Portugal's flagship grape, intensely floral and concentrated, long the secret muscle behind great Port. Increasingly spotted flying solo as a dry table wine.
funFact: Touriga Nacional yields tiny, thick-skinned berries and famously stingy crops, which is exactly why it anchors the blends of vintage Port.

name: Zinfandel
description: A Croatian native that migrated to California and went gloriously feral, ripening into brambly, high-octane jamminess. Gnarled old-vine specimens over a century old still roam Lodi and Sonoma.
funFact: In 2001, DNA sleuths traced Zinfandel to the obscure Croatian grape Crljenak Kaštelanski, proving it identical to Italy's Primitivo.

name: Amarone della Valpolicella
description: Born from grapes dried on racks for months before fermentation, concentrating them into a rich, raisin-edged giant. Velvety, potent, and best approached after dinner is already underway.
funFact: Amarone means roughly 'the great bitter,' a name coined to distinguish this dry wine from Recioto, the sweet style it accidentally evolved from when a barrel fermented fully dry.

name: Barolo
description: Nebbiolo's final evolution, achieved only on the Langhe hills after years of mandatory aging. Pale in color, colossal in structure, haunted by tar and roses.
funFact: Italian law requires Barolo to age at least 38 months before release, and it has long been called 'the wine of kings and the king of wines.'

name: Bordeaux Blend
description: A team composition perfected over centuries: Cabernet Sauvignon for structure, Merlot for flesh, with Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, and Malbec in support. Imitated on every continent that grows grapes.
funFact: American producers coined the term 'Meritage' — rhyming with 'heritage' — in 1988 to name New World wines built from Bordeaux grape varieties.

name: Brunello di Montalcino
description: Sangiovese in its most patient and powerful form, grown on a single Tuscan hilltop and aged for years before it may leave home. Rewards those who wait even longer.
funFact: Brunello cannot legally be sold until January 1 of the fifth year after harvest, and it was among the first Italian wines awarded DOCG status in 1980.

name: Châteauneuf-du-Pape
description: A warm, spicy Grenache-led blend from stony vineyards once tended for the popes of Avignon. Up to thirteen grape varieties may join the party.
funFact: In 1954 the village council passed a decree banning flying saucers from landing in its vineyards, with any offending craft to be impounded — the decree still stands.

name: Chianti
description: Tuscany's Sangiovese-based table companion, once famous for its straw-basket fiasco bottle. Tart cherry and dusty herbs, engineered by centuries of pairing with pasta.
funFact: A 1716 edict by Cosimo III de' Medici drew official boundaries around Chianti, making it one of the world's first legally delimited wine regions.

name: Côte-Rôtie
description: Syrah from vertiginous terraced slopes so steep they must be worked by hand, perfumed with violets and smoked meat. The 'roasted slope' earns its name every summer.
funFact: Producers may legally co-ferment up to 20% of the white grape Viognier with Syrah here — a rare red-white marriage enshrined in French appellation law.

name: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo
description: Central Italy's friendly, inky trattoria staple: soft tannins, dark plummy fruit, and a price that encourages a second bottle. Rarely demands attention; always earns it.
funFact: Despite the name, the Montepulciano grape has nothing to do with the Tuscan town of Montepulciano, whose famous wine is made from Sangiovese instead.

name: Priorat
description: Old-vine Garnacha and Cariñena clawing a living from black slate hillsides in Catalonia. The resulting wines are dense, mineral, and unapologetically powerful.
funFact: Priorat is one of only two Spanish regions granted top-tier DOCa/DOQ status (the other is Rioja), with vines rooted in a glittering slate soil called llicorella.

name: Rioja
description: Tempranillo raised in American oak until it emerges smelling of vanilla, coconut, and old libraries. Its Crianza–Reserva–Gran Reserva ranking system tells you how long it slumbered.
funFact: In 1991, Rioja became the first Spanish region elevated to DOCa status, the country's highest wine classification.

name: Provence Rosé
description: The pale-pink standard-bearer of all rosé: dry, delicate, and the color of onion skin at sunset. Migrates in enormous numbers to patios every summer.
funFact: Rosé makes up roughly nine in ten bottles produced in Provence, France's oldest wine region, first planted by Greek settlers around 600 BC.

name: Tavel
description: The serious one of the rosé family: dark-hued, full-bodied, and structured enough to face down a steak. Its home appellation in the Rhône makes nothing else.
funFact: Tavel is one of the few French appellations devoted exclusively to rosé, and it counted Ernest Hemingway among its devoted drinkers.

name: White Zinfandel
description: A sweet, blush-pink pour born from a happy winemaking accident in 1970s California. Wine snobs scoff, but it kept America's old Zinfandel vines in the ground.
funFact: It was created in 1975 when a Zinfandel fermentation stuck, leaving residual sugar in a pale pink wine that went on to become a massive commercial hit.

name: Daiginjo
description: The top of the sake pyramid, brewed from rice grains milled down to half their size or less. Silky, perfumed, and best served chilled in delicate glassware.
funFact: Some ambitious brewers polish away more than 70% of each rice grain, leaving only the pure starchy heart of the kernel to ferment.

name: Ginjo
description: A fragrant, fruit-forward sake grade whose rice is polished to 60% or less of its original size before brewing. Long, cold fermentation coaxes out aromas of melon and green apple.
funFact: Ginjo's signature fruity aromas come from special yeast strains fermenting at low temperatures — the same ester compounds found in real apples and bananas.

name: Honjozo
description: A light, easy-drinking sake grade brewed with a small measured addition of distilled alcohol, which lifts aromas and dries out the finish. A favorite for warming on cold nights.
funFact: The added brewer's alcohol isn't a cheap filler in honjozo — it's strictly limited by law and used to make the sake lighter and more fragrant.

name: Junmai
description: The pure-rice class of sake: nothing but rice, water, koji mold, and yeast. Fuller and more savory than its polished siblings, and excellent gently warmed.
funFact: Sake is brewed via 'multiple parallel fermentation' — starch converts to sugar and sugar to alcohol simultaneously in one tank, a process unique among major beverages.

name: Nigori
description: Cloudy sake, coarsely filtered so that soft rice particles stay swirling in the bottle like a snow globe. Creamy, gently sweet, and requires a shake before pouring.
funFact: The word 'nigori' literally means 'cloudy' in Japanese, and the style is the closest modern descendant of the rustic, unfiltered sake of centuries past.

name: Amontillado Sherry
description: A sherry with two lives: it begins under protective flor like a fino, then loses its yeast shield and ages exposed to air. The result is amber, nutty, and quietly complex.
funFact: Edgar Allan Poe made this style infamous in his 1846 tale 'The Cask of Amontillado,' in which a wine lover is lured to his doom by the promise of a taste.

name: Cream Sherry
description: An oloroso sweetened into plush, toffee-toned comfort, long the gateway sherry of grandmotherly sideboards. Modern bartenders have quietly rediscovered its charms over ice.
funFact: The style was created for the British market, and the term 'cream' was popularized in Bristol as a plusher successor to the older blend known as 'Bristol Milk.'

name: Fino Sherry
description: Bone-dry sherry raised beneath flor, a living blanket of yeast that guards it from air. Emerges pale, saline, and almond-tinged — the driest creature in the bodega.
funFact: The flor yeast that shapes fino consumes the wine's glycerin and residual sugar as it protects it, which is why fino tastes so strikingly dry and lean.

name: Manzanilla Sherry
description: Fino's coastal cousin, aged only in one seaside town where ocean air keeps its yeast blanket thriving. Drinkers swear they taste salt spray and chamomile in every sip.
funFact: Manzanilla may only be aged in Sanlúcar de Barrameda, where humid Atlantic air keeps the flor yeast alive and vigorous year-round.

name: Oloroso Sherry
description: Fortified high from the start so no yeast can shield it, this sherry ages in open combat with oxygen. Decades later it emerges dark, walnut-rich, and structurally imposing.
funFact: Oloroso means 'fragrant' in Spanish; the style is fortified above 17% precisely so that flor yeast cannot survive on its surface.

name: Palo Cortado Sherry
description: The bodega's happy accident: a wine that set out to become fino but lost its flor and drifted toward oloroso richness. It keeps amontillado's finesse and oloroso's body.
funFact: Its name means 'cut stick,' after the chalk mark cellar masters slash across casks whose flor has unexpectedly died, rerouting the wine to oxidative aging.

name: Pedro Ximénez Sherry
description: Grapes sun-dried to near-raisins before pressing yield a black, syrupy elixir of fig and molasses. Less a beverage than a dessert that happens to pour.
funFact: PX can exceed 400 grams of sugar per liter, and in Spain it is famously poured straight over vanilla ice cream.

name: Orange Wine
description: White wine made like a red: the juice ferments on its grape skins for days or months, emerging amber-hued, tannic, and faintly wild. Contains no oranges whatsoever.
funFact: The technique traces back roughly 8,000 years to Georgia, where wine is still fermented in buried clay vessels called qvevri — a method inscribed on UNESCO's cultural heritage list.

name: Cava
description: Spain's bottle-fermented answer to Champagne, made mostly in Catalonia from a trio of local grapes. Delivers toasty traditional-method character at a friendly price.
funFact: The name simply means 'cellar' in Catalan, after the underground caves where the bottles age; the classic blend is Macabeo, Xarel·lo, and Parellada.

name: Champagne
description: The apex predator of sparkling wine, born of a second fermentation inside each bottle in France's chilly northeast. Its very name is guarded by law worldwide.
funFact: The pressure inside a Champagne bottle reaches about six atmospheres — roughly triple the pressure in a car tire.

name: Crémant
description: France's family of traditional-method sparklers made everywhere except Champagne — Alsace, the Loire, Burgundy, and beyond. The insider's route to fine French bubbles.
funFact: There are eight Crémant appellations across France, from Crémant d'Alsace to Crémant de Limoux, all using Champagne's bottle-fermentation method.

name: English Sparkling Wine
description: A cool-climate upstart from the chalk hills of southern England that has taken to beating Champagne in blind tastings. Crisp, taut, and quietly smug about the whole thing.
funFact: The chalk downs of southern England belong to the same geological basin as the chalk beneath Champagne, just across the Channel.

name: Franciacorta
description: Italy's most serious sparkling wine, bottle-fermented in Lombardy from Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. It rarely leaves Italy, where locals happily drink most of it themselves.
funFact: Non-vintage Franciacorta must age at least 18 months on its lees in bottle — longer than the 12 months required for non-vintage Champagne.

name: Lambrusco
description: A frothing purple sparkler from Emilia-Romagna, engineered by generations of Italians to cut through plates of salumi and lasagna. Dry versions bear no resemblance to its sugary 1980s reputation.
funFact: In the late 1970s and 1980s, sweet Lambrusco was the best-selling imported wine in the United States.

name: Pét-Nat
description: Short for pétillant naturel: wine bottled before its first fermentation finishes, trapping bubbles the ancestral way. Often cloudy, usually crown-capped, always a little unpredictable.
funFact: The ancestral method behind pét-nat predates Champagne's technique — monks at Saint-Hilaire near Limoux were making sparkling wine this way in the 1500s.

name: Prosecco
description: Italy's cheerful, pear-scented fizz, made from the Glera grape and carbonated in big steel tanks rather than bottles. The engine behind every Aperol Spritz.
funFact: Prosecco takes its name from a small village near Trieste, though most of it now comes from vineyards between Conegliano and Valdobbiadene.

name: Sekt
description: Germany's homegrown sparkler, at its best when made from Riesling with racy acidity and orchard fruit. Most of it never escapes the German-speaking world.
funFact: Germans are among the world's biggest per-capita drinkers of sparkling wine, which explains why so little Sekt is left over to export.

name: Dry Vermouth
description: The pale, herbal French counterpart to Italy's sweet style, crisp with alpine botanicals and citrus. Best known as the whispering partner in a Martini.
funFact: The dry French style was developed around 1813 by Joseph Noilly, whose Noilly Prat remains the benchmark bartenders reach for in a classic Martini.

name: Sweet Vermouth
description: Wine aromatized with wormwood, spices, and bittersweet botanicals in the Italian style. Equally content stirred into a Negroni or served alone over ice with an orange slice, as Turin intended.
funFact: Modern sweet vermouth was born in Turin in 1786 at the shop of Antonio Benedetto Carpano, and the word 'vermouth' comes from 'Wermut,' German for wormwood.

name: Albariño
description: A saline, citrusy coastal dweller from Spain's rainy northwest, seemingly engineered by nature to accompany shellfish. Often carries a whisper of sea spray.
funFact: Across the border in Portugal the same grape is called Alvarinho, where it stars in the finest bottlings of Vinho Verde.

name: Assyrtiko
description: A volcanic survivor from Santorini that keeps razor acidity even under scorching Aegean sun. Bone dry, smoky, and startlingly saline.
funFact: On windswept Santorini, Assyrtiko vines are woven into low basket shapes called kouloura, with the grapes growing inside for protection.

name: Chablis
description: Chardonnay stripped to its skeleton: steely, saline, and rarely troubled by oak. It grows in cold northern Burgundy atop ancient seabed.
funFact: Chablis vines grow in Kimmeridgian limestone studded with fossilized oyster shells from a sea that covered the region 150 million years ago.

name: Chardonnay
description: The great shape-shifter of white grapes, appearing lean and steely in cool cellars yet golden and buttery wherever oak barrels lurk. Found on virtually every wine list on Earth.
funFact: DNA analysis at UC Davis revealed Chardonnay is a natural cross between noble Pinot Noir and the humble medieval grape Gouais Blanc.

name: Chenin Blanc
description: The Loire's do-everything grape, capable of dry, sweet, still, and sparkling forms without breaking a sweat. Its searing acidity lets great examples age for half a century.
funFact: South Africa grows more Chenin Blanc than France does, where the grape has long gone by the local name 'Steen'.

name: Gewürztraminer
description: An unmistakably perfumed specimen that smells of lychee and rose petals before you even lift the glass. Loud, golden, and impossible to confuse with anything else.
funFact: The grape takes its name from the village of Tramin in the Italian Alps, with 'Gewürz' meaning 'spice' in German.

name: Grüner Veltliner
description: Austria's signature white, zippy and green-tinged with a telltale flick of white pepper on the finish. A sommelier favorite for its uncanny food friendliness.
funFact: Its peppery bite comes from rotundone, the same aroma compound found in actual black peppercorns and in Syrah.

name: Muscadet
description: A briny, feather-light white from the Atlantic mouth of the Loire, made from the Melon de Bourgogne grape. It exists in near-perfect symbiosis with raw oysters.
funFact: Bottles labeled 'sur lie' rest on their spent yeast cells through the winter, picking up a subtle creaminess and a faint natural spritz.

name: Picpoul de Pinet
description: A zesty Mediterranean white from the lagoons of the Languedoc, traditionally shipped in a distinctive tall green bottle. Built for oysters farmed within sight of its vines.
funFact: The grape's name, Piquepoul, translates roughly to 'lip stinger' — a nod to its bracing acidity.

name: Pinot Grigio
description: A light, breezy sipper that evolved from a grayish-pink mutation of Pinot Noir. In its Italian form it is crisp and neutral; as Alsatian Pinot Gris it grows richer and spicier.
funFact: Pinot Grigio and Pinot Gris are the exact same grape — the 'gris' (gray) refers to the oddly grayish-blue tint of its skins.

name: Retsina
description: An ancient Greek oddity infused with pine resin during fermentation, giving it an unmistakable forest-floor perfume. Divisive, historic, and stubbornly still here.
funFact: The style descends from antiquity, when amphorae were sealed with pine resin and the flavor seeped into the wine — Greeks came to like it that way.

name: Riesling
description: A high-acid chameleon that ranges from bone dry to nectar sweet while somehow always tasting like itself. With age it develops a curious and prized whiff of petrol.
funFact: Riesling's first documented mention dates to 1435, in the cellar inventory of a German count at Rüsselsheim.

name: Sancerre
description: The most aristocratic form of Sauvignon Blanc, grown on flint and limestone hills overlooking the upper Loire. Smoky, precise, and perpetually in demand at wine bars.
funFact: Though famous for whites, the Sancerre appellation also covers reds and rosés made from Pinot Noir, a remnant of its pre-phylloxera past as red wine country.

name: Sauvignon Blanc
description: A sharp, grassy creature that announces itself from across the room with a burst of gooseberry and cut grass. Thrives in the Loire, Marlborough, and refrigerators worldwide.
funFact: Its name derives from the French 'sauvage' (wild), and it is a parent of Cabernet Sauvignon via a chance crossing with Cabernet Franc.

name: Sémillon
description: A quiet, waxy grape that plays two extremes: the backbone of golden Sauternes in Bordeaux, and a lean, ageless dry white in Australia's Hunter Valley.
funFact: Hunter Valley Sémillon is picked early at low alcohol and tastes almost neutral in youth, then miraculously develops honeyed, toasty depth over decades in bottle.

name: Soave
description: A gentle Venetian white built on the Garganega grape, all pear and almond softened by volcanic soils. Once dismissed as cheap, its hillside crus are quietly excellent.
funFact: In the 1970s Soave was the best-selling imported Italian wine in the United States, outselling even Chianti.

name: Torrontés
description: Argentina's aromatic trickster: it smells sweet as a flower shop, then lands crisp and dry. Happiest in dizzyingly high desert vineyards.
funFact: Torrontés is a natural cross between Muscat of Alexandria and the Mission grape brought to the Americas by Spanish missionaries.

name: Txakoli
description: The Basque Country's electric, lightly fizzy white, low in alcohol and high in theatrics. Bartenders pour it from a great height to rouse its bubbles.
funFact: In San Sebastián's pintxo bars, Txakoli is traditionally poured from arm's length above the glass to aerate it and coax out its natural fizz.

name: Vermentino
description: A sun-loving Mediterranean white with a pleasantly bitter, almond-skin farewell. It patrols the coasts of Sardinia, Liguria, and Corsica, where it moonlights as Rolle.
funFact: Vermentino di Gallura is the only DOCG, Italy's highest wine classification, on the entire island of Sardinia.

name: Vinho Verde
description: Portugal's 'green wine' — green as in young, not in color. Low in alcohol, lightly spritzy, and best consumed within sight of a beach.
funFact: The gentle fizz was originally an accident of secondary fermentation in bottle; today many producers add a small dose of carbon dioxide on purpose.

name: Viognier
description: A lush, apricot-scented rarity rescued from the brink of extinction. Full-bodied and heady, it walks the line between opulence and excess.
funFact: By the 1960s Viognier had dwindled to roughly a dozen acres in Condrieu before a global revival brought it back from near extinction.

name: Bacanora
description: Sonora's clandestine agave spirit, distilled from wild agave in mountain hideouts through nearly eight decades of prohibition. Smoky, mineral, and still carrying the swagger of the outlaw years.
funFact: Bacanora was outlawed in Sonora from 1915 until 1992, so generations of families kept the tradition alive with hidden stills in the sierra.

name: Mezcal Añejo
description: Mezcal aged at least a year in oak, where smoke, caramel, and leather negotiate a rich truce. A rarity, since most mezcaleros prefer their spirit young and untamed.
funFact: Unlike tequila's single permitted species, mezcal may legally be produced from dozens of different agave varieties.

name: Mezcal de Pechuga
description: Ceremonial mezcal given a final distillation with seasonal fruits, spices, and a raw poultry breast suspended in the still. Brewed for weddings and saints' days, encountered by mortals almost never.
funFact: 'Pechuga' means 'breast' — traditionally a whole chicken or turkey breast hangs inside the still during the final pass, subtly rounding the spirit.

name: Mezcal Joven
description: Unaged mezcal, where agave hearts roasted in earthen pits deliver their famous campfire smoke and wild fruit. Oaxaca's rawest, truest voice.
funFact: Mezcal's signature smokiness comes from roasting agave hearts for days in stone-lined pits dug into the earth.

name: Mezcal Reposado
description: Mezcal rested briefly in wood, letting vanilla and honey settle over the smoke like dusk over a cookfire. A gentler on-ramp to the smoky arts.
funFact: Around nine in every ten bottles of mezcal are made from a single cultivated agave, espadín, prized for its relatively quick maturation.

name: Mezcal Tobalá
description: Mezcal from the small, wild tobalá agave that hides in high mountain canyons and yields only a fraction of what farmed espadín gives. Often crowned 'the king of mezcals.'
funFact: Tobalá agave produces no clones or offshoots — it reproduces only by seed in the wild, which is a big reason it stays scarce and expensive.

name: Raicilla
description: West Jalisco's backwoods agave spirit, long distilled off the books in the sierra and along the coast — funky, fruity, and less smoky than its Oaxacan cousins. Mezcal's mischievous mountain kin.
funFact: Raicilla — 'little root' — reputedly got its name as a colonial-era tax dodge, and it finally received its own denomination of origin in 2019.

name: Sotol
description: The spirit of the Chihuahuan Desert, distilled from the wild desert spoon plant into something grassy, mineral, and quietly feral. Tastes like the high desert after rain.
funFact: Despite being shelved with agave spirits, sotol is not made from agave at all — the desert spoon is a different plant that can take around 15 years to mature.

name: Tequila Añejo
description: Tequila aged one to three years, trading youthful bite for caramel, chocolate, and dried fruit. Proof that agave can play in whiskey's league.
funFact: By law, añejo must age in oak barrels no larger than 600 liters, which keeps the wood's influence concentrated.

name: Tequila Blanco
description: Tequila in its purest form, bottled fresh from the still so the roasted blue agave speaks without oak interrupting. Peppery, vegetal, and vividly alive.
funFact: A blue Weber agave typically grows for six to eight years before a jimador harvests its heart, called the piña for its resemblance to a pineapple.

name: Tequila Cristalino
description: Aged tequila filtered through charcoal until it runs crystal clear, keeping barrel softness while shedding barrel color. Alchemy for drinkers who want their añejo invisible.
funFact: The cristalino craze is usually traced to Don Julio 70, launched in 2011 as the first widely marketed clear añejo.

name: Tequila Extra Añejo
description: Ultra-aged tequila that slumbers in oak for at least three years, emerging dark, plush, and cognac-like. The category tequila invented once it started wearing suits.
funFact: Extra añejo is the newest official tequila classification, created only in 2006 as producers pushed into luxury territory.

name: Tequila Joven
description: The 'young' or gold style, usually a blanco softened with a splash of aged tequila or a touch of color and sweetness. The tequila of a million spring-break stories.
funFact: Most inexpensive 'gold' tequila gets its color from added caramel coloring rather than from time spent in a barrel.

name: Tequila Reposado
description: Tequila 'rested' in oak for two months to a year, just long enough to drape vanilla and soft spice over the agave without smothering it. The diplomatic middle ground.
funFact: Reposado literally means 'rested,' and much of the resting happens in used American bourbon barrels shipped south across the border.

name: Aperol
description: Campari's sunnier, gentler sibling, glowing neon orange and only lightly bitter. In spritz form it has colonized patios across the entire planet.
funFact: Aperol was created in 1919 by brothers Luigi and Silvio Barbieri of Padua and carries roughly half the alcohol of its rival Campari.

name: Campari
description: The scarlet gatekeeper of the aperitivo hour, bitter as a grudge and bright as a sunset. It tests new trainers with grapefruit-pith bitterness before rewarding them for life.
funFact: Campari's famous red color came from carmine dye made from cochineal insects until the company switched to artificial coloring in 2006.

name: Cynar
description: An amaro that proudly wears an artichoke on its label, yet tastes of caramelized herbs rather than vegetables. A gentle, vegetal riddle beloved in low-proof cocktails.
funFact: Launched in 1952, Cynar takes its name from Cynara scolymus, the artichoke, one of thirteen herbs and plants in its recipe.

name: Fernet-Branca
description: A menthol-black Italian amaro of legendary intensity, brewed from 27 secret herbs. Feared by novices, worshipped by bartenders, and consumed by Argentina in heroic quantities.
funFact: Argentina drinks well over 70% of all Fernet-Branca produced, mostly mixed with cola in the beloved fernet con coca.

name: American Single Malt
description: One hundred percent malted barley from a single American distillery — Scotland's blueprint rebuilt with New World swagger. The newest official branch of the whiskey family tree.
funFact: American single malt only became an officially recognized U.S. whiskey category when the TTB finalized its rule in December 2024.

name: Bottled-in-Bond Bourbon
description: Whiskey with a government-stamped pedigree: one distillery, one distilling season, at least four years in a bonded warehouse, and exactly 100 proof. No fudging allowed.
funFact: The Bottled-in-Bond Act of 1897 was one of America's earliest consumer-protection laws, arriving nine years before the Pure Food and Drug Act.

name: Bourbon
description: America's signature whiskey, born of a corn-heavy mash and new charred oak. Sweet, sturdy, and sociable — it appears anywhere Americans gather to argue about whiskey.
funFact: In 1964 the U.S. Congress declared bourbon a distinctive product of the United States, though it can legally be made in any state, not just Kentucky.

name: Cask Strength Bourbon
description: Bourbon bottled straight from the barrel with no dilution — whiskey with the volume knob snapped off. Approach with water, patience, or bravado.
funFact: Bourbon may legally enter the barrel at no more than 125 proof, but years of evaporation in hot rickhouses can push some barrel-proof releases above 70% ABV.

name: Flavored Whiskey
description: Whiskey infused with cinnamon, honey, apple, or peach, engineered to go down like dessert. Purists scowl; sales figures do not.
funFact: Flavored whiskeys are often bottled below the 40% ABV minimum required of straight whiskey, which is why the flavor designation must appear on the label.

name: High-Rye Bourbon
description: Still legally bourbon, but with the rye content cranked toward the ceiling for extra snap and spice. The bridge species between bourbon and rye whiskey.
funFact: One of Four Roses' two mash bills contains 35% rye — among the highest rye content of any major bourbon on the market.

name: Moonshine
description: Unaged white whiskey with an outlaw pedigree, once run through the hollows in mason jars ahead of the revenuers. Today's legal versions keep the jar and skip the felony.
funFact: The name comes from distilling illegally by the light of the moon to avoid detection by tax collectors.

name: Rye Whiskey
description: Bourbon's spicier, drier sibling, distilled from a mash of at least 51% rye grain. It bites first and charms second, which is exactly why bartenders adore it.
funFact: Before Prohibition, rye — not bourbon — was the dominant American whiskey, with Pennsylvania's Monongahela Valley as its most famous producing region.

name: Single Barrel Bourbon
description: Every bottle drawn from one lone barrel, so no two barrels taste quite alike. Catching a great one is half the sport.
funFact: Blanton's, created in 1984 by master distiller Elmer T. Lee, is widely credited as the first modern bourbon marketed as a single-barrel bottling.

name: Small Batch Bourbon
description: A curated blend of a modest number of barrels, aiming for a house flavor with a handcrafted halo. The batch is small; the marketing rarely is.
funFact: The term 'small batch' has no legal definition in the United States — a batch can be any number of barrels the producer decides to call small.

name: Straight Corn Whiskey
description: Made from at least 80% corn and aged only in used or uncharred oak, keeping the grain's sweet, popcorn-like soul front and center. A living fossil of early American distilling.
funFact: Corn whiskey is the only major American whiskey style that is forbidden from using new charred oak barrels — the very thing that defines bourbon.

name: Tennessee Whiskey
description: Essentially a bourbon that takes a detour through sugar-maple charcoal before barreling, emerging mellower for the trip. Tennessee guards this ritual jealously.
funFact: A 2013 Tennessee state law requires whiskey labeled 'Tennessee whiskey' to use the charcoal-mellowing Lincoln County Process, with a grandfathered exception for one small distillery.

name: Wheat Whiskey
description: Not a wheated bourbon but a true wheat-majority whiskey, soft and bready with a gentle sweetness. A quiet rarity in a category built on corn.
funFact: Wheat whiskey must contain at least 51% wheat in the mash, making it a legally distinct category from wheated bourbon, which remains majority corn.

name: Wheated Bourbon
description: A bourbon that swaps rye for wheat as its flavoring grain, trading spice for a soft, bakery-sweet roundness. Gentle in youth, glorious in old age.
funFact: The cult favorite Pappy Van Winkle is a wheated bourbon, and its scarcity helped turn the whole 'wheater' style into a collector obsession.

name: Absinthe
description: The infamous Green Fairy: a potent wormwood-and-anise spirit that louches to opalescent cloud with water. Long blamed for madness it never actually caused.
funFact: Absinthe was banned in the United States from 1912 until 2007; modern science showed its supposed hallucinogenic powers were a myth all along.

name: Arak
description: The Levant's grape-and-anise spirit, triple-distilled and diluted at the table until it swirls milky white. It presides over mezze spreads like a benevolent elder.
funFact: The name arak comes from the Arabic word for 'sweat' or 'perspiration,' a nod to the drops of condensed spirit dripping from the still.

name: Ouzo
description: Greece's crystal-clear anise spirit that turns ghostly white with water or ice. It appears wherever grilled octopus, sea breezes, and long afternoons are found.
funFact: Under EU law, ouzo can only be produced in Greece and Cyprus, making it a protected badge of Greek identity.

name: Pastis
description: The licorice-scented soul of Marseille, born to fill the void when absinthe was banned. Splashed with cold water it blooms milky yellow, and suddenly it is summer in Provence.
funFact: Paul Ricard launched his namesake pastis in 1932, marketing it as 'the true pastis of Marseille' in the wake of France's absinthe ban.

name: Rakı
description: Turkey's national anise spirit, distilled from grapes and raisins. Mixed with water it clouds into the fabled 'lion's milk,' fueling long tables of meze and conversation.
funFact: Rakı is affectionately nicknamed 'aslan sütü,' or lion's milk, for the milky white color it takes on when mixed with water.

name: Sambuca
description: Italy's syrupy anise liqueur, served neat, flaming, or floating three coffee beans. Sweeter and heavier than its Greek and French cousins, with a theatrical streak.
funFact: Sambuca served 'con la mosca' ('with the fly') comes with three coffee beans representing health, happiness, and prosperity.

name: American Brandy
description: Grape brandy from the United States, long dominated by sunny California workhorses and lately reinvigorated by a wave of craft pot-still upstarts. An old category enjoying a second act.
funFact: Christian Brothers brandy was genuinely made by a Catholic teaching order — the De La Salle Christian Brothers — who used the profits to fund their schools.

name: Applejack
description: Colonial America's apple brandy, once conjured by leaving hard cider out to freeze and skimming off the ice. The young republic ran on this stuff.
funFact: Early American farmers made applejack by 'jacking' — freeze-concentrating hard cider in winter and removing the ice, no still required.

name: Armagnac
description: Gascony's rustic country brandy, usually run just once through a peculiar traveling column still and left to gather prune-and-violet depth for decades. Cognac's older, earthier cousin who stayed on the farm.
funFact: A treatise written around 1310 praises the medicinal virtues of Gascon 'burning water,' making Armagnac France's oldest documented brandy — well before cognac.

name: Brandy de Jerez
description: Andalusian brandy raised in casks soaked with decades of sherry, gathering raisin, fig, and nutty richness as it cascades through the solera. Sunshine, but aged.
funFact: Brandy de Jerez must be aged within the 'sherry triangle' of Andalusia, in ex-sherry casks, using the same solera system that ages the region's famous wines.

name: Calvados
description: Normandy's orchard in a bottle: cider apples (and sometimes pears) fermented, distilled, and aged into autumn itself. France's answer to the question of what to do without vineyards.
funFact: The 'trou normand' — the Norman hole — is the tradition of downing a mid-feast shot of calvados to make room for the next course.

name: Cognac VS
description: The youngest official grade of France's most famous grape brandy, twice-distilled in copper pots and aged at least two years. Bright, grapey, and happiest in a mixed drink.
funFact: Cognac's age grades carry English initials — VS stands for 'Very Special' — a legacy of Britain's centuries-long role as the region's biggest customer.

name: Cognac VSOP
description: Cognac's comfortable middle chapter, aged at least four years into rounder fruit and warmer spice. The bottle most likely to appear when someone says 'the good stuff.'
funFact: VSOP — 'Very Superior Old Pale' — traces back to an 1817 order in which Britain's future King George IV requested exactly such a cognac from Hennessy.

name: Cognac XO
description: 'Extra Old' cognac, where long-slumbering eaux-de-vie develop the walnut-and-candied-fruit depth the French call rancio. Made for slow evenings and slower sips.
funFact: In April 2018 the minimum age of the youngest brandy in an XO blend was raised from six years to ten.

name: French Brandy
description: Grape brandy made in France outside the hallowed boundaries of Cognac and Armagnac, usually column-distilled, softly sweet, and honestly priced. The everyday pour of the brandy world.
funFact: European law reserves the name 'Cognac' for the delimited Charente region — identical grapes distilled just outside the boundary can only ever be labeled brandy.

name: Grappa
description: Italy's thrifty masterpiece, distilled not from wine but from the skins, seeds, and stems left after pressing. Once fierce peasant fuel, now a refined digestivo.
funFact: Under European law the name grappa is reserved for pomace spirit produced in Italy, San Marino, or Italian-speaking Switzerland.

name: Kirschwasser
description: A crystal-clear cherry eau-de-vie from the Black Forest, distilled with the fruit's pits for a whisper of bitter almond. Cherries, distilled down to their ghost.
funFact: Under German food guidelines an authentic Schwarzwälder Kirschtorte — Black Forest cake — must actually contain kirschwasser to bear the name.

name: Pálinka
description: Hungary's fiercely protected fruit brandy, distilled purely from apricots, plums, pears, or cherries with nothing added — not even sugar. Fruit, fire, and national pride.
funFact: EU law reserves the name pálinka for fruit spirits made in Hungary, with a lone exception for apricot spirit from four Austrian provinces.

name: Pisco
description: South America's aromatic grape brandy, distilled from fragrant muscat-family varieties and, in Peru, never touched by oak. Floral, potent, and the engine of a famous sour.
funFact: Peru and Chile both claim pisco as their national spirit, and each country legally restricts the name to its own production within its borders.

name: Poire Williams
description: Pear eau-de-vie of startling purity, capturing the perfume of a ripe Williams pear in water-clear spirit. The fanciest bottles come with a full-grown pear trapped inside.
funFact: To get a whole pear inside the bottle, producers hang empty bottles on the trees in spring so the fruit grows to maturity within the glass.

name: Slivovitz
description: The plum brandy of Central Europe and the Balkans, distilled at countless family stills and poured at every wedding, funeral, and Tuesday. Hospitality with a kick.
funFact: The social practices around preparing Serbia's plum spirit šljivovica were inscribed on UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage list in 2022.

name: Batavia Arrack
description: An ancient Javanese cane spirit with a smoky, funky soul, fermented with the help of red rice cakes. A fossil species from the golden age of punch, recently revived.
funFact: Batavia arrack was a cornerstone of 18th-century punch bowls and remains the defining ingredient in Sweden's traditional punsch liqueur.

name: Cachaça
description: Brazil's national spirit, distilled from fresh sugarcane juice with a bright, vegetal swagger. It is the beating heart of the caipirinha and refuses to be called rum.
funFact: In 2013 the United States formally agreed to recognize cachaça as a distinctive Brazilian product, so only spirits made in Brazil can carry the name there.

name: Pitorro
description: Puerto Rico's clandestine cane spirit, traditionally distilled in hidden backyard stills and buried underground to mellow. Often infused with tropical fruit and broken out at Christmas.
funFact: Pitorro is the soul of coquito season: families steep it with fruit for months, and the buried-jug aging ritual earned it the nickname 'pitorro curao' (cured pitorro).

name: Barrel-Aged Gin
description: Gin that ventured into oak and came back wearing amber armor. Vanilla and spice soften the juniper, creating a hybrid creature that flirts with whiskey territory.
funFact: Aged gin is really a throwback: before glass bottles were cheap, gin and genever routinely traveled and rested in wooden casks that colored the spirit.

name: Contemporary Gin
description: A modern mutation of gin that turns the juniper down and the botanicals up: cucumber, rose, citrus, or tea may take the lead. The species responsible for gin's 21st-century boom.
funFact: The style label 'New Western Dry Gin' was coined by distiller Ryan Magarian to describe gins where juniper shares the stage with other botanicals.

name: Genever
description: The malty Dutch progenitor of all gin, part whisky-like grain spirit and part juniper elixir. A living fossil that predates its famous descendant by centuries.
funFact: The phrase 'Dutch courage' is said to come from English soldiers drinking genever before battle alongside their Dutch allies in the 17th century.

name: London Dry Gin
description: The crisp, juniper-forward alpha of the gin family. Bone dry and bracing, it anchors the martini and the gin and tonic with piney authority.
funFact: Despite the name, London dry is a production style rather than a place of origin, so a London dry gin can legally be made anywhere in the world.

name: Navy Strength Gin
description: Gin's armored battle form, bottled at a formidable 57% or more. Built for cocktails that need juniper to punch through citrus and ice without flinching.
funFact: At 57% ABV, gunpowder soaked with the gin will still ignite, the historic Royal Navy test that gave 'navy strength' its name.

name: Old Tom Gin
description: A softer, sweeter ancestor of London dry that prowled 18th-century England. Thought extinct for decades, it was revived to complete classic recipes like the Tom Collins and Martinez.
funFact: Legend says the name comes from black cat ('Old Tom') plaques on pub walls, where a coin in a slot bought a shot of gin dispensed through a tube.

name: Sloe Gin
description: A ruby-red liqueur form of gin, created by steeping tart blackthorn sloes in spirit with sugar. Hedgerow foragers' treasure, equally at home in a flute or a flask.
funFact: Tradition holds that sloes should be picked after the first frost, which softens the berries' skins and mellows their fierce astringency.

name: Bénédictine
description: A honeyed French liqueur of 27 herbs and spices wrapped in monastic mystique. Its palace-like distillery in Normandy is as theatrical as the spirit is smooth.
funFact: The world's biggest single consumer of Bénédictine is reputedly the Burnley Miners' Club in Lancashire, England, a taste local soldiers brought home from World War I.

name: Drambuie
description: Scotch whisky gilded with heather honey, herbs, and spice. A golden Highland treasure whose destiny is fulfilled the moment it meets more Scotch in a Rusty Nail.
funFact: Legend holds that Bonnie Prince Charlie gave the secret recipe to the MacKinnon clan as thanks for sheltering him after the failed 1745 Jacobite rising.

name: Génépi
description: An alpine liqueur distilled from tiny artemisia flowers that cling to high mountain scree. Ski-lodge medicine with a bittersweet, wormwood-kissed bite.
funFact: The génépi plants used in the liqueur grow only at high altitude, and gathering the wild flowers is restricted in parts of the Alps to protect them.

name: Green Chartreuse
description: A luminous green elixir of some 130 plants, brewed by silent Carthusian monks in the French Alps. So iconic that the color chartreuse is named after it, and lately as hard to catch as any legendary.
funFact: Only two Carthusian monks at a time are said to know the complete recipe, which traces back to a mysterious manuscript given to the order in 1605.

name: Yellow Chartreuse
description: The mellower golden evolution of Green Chartreuse, sweetened with honey and softened with saffron. It trades its sibling's fire for a warm, glowing calm.
funFact: Yellow Chartreuse was introduced by the monks in 1838 as a milder, sweeter companion to the original green formula.

name: Irish Blended Whiskey
description: Smooth, approachable whiskey blending pot still, malt, and grain spirit, typically triple-distilled into famous friendliness. The gateway through which most drinkers meet Ireland.
funFact: Irish whiskey was the world's most popular whiskey in the 1800s, then collapsed so completely that by the 1970s the entire island had only two working distilleries.

name: Irish Single Malt
description: All malted barley from a single Irish distillery, usually triple-distilled and almost always unpeated — orchard fruit and honey where Scotland might offer smoke.
funFact: The Old Bushmills Distillery traces its licence to distil to 1608, a date often cited as making it the oldest licensed whiskey distillery in the world.

name: Irish Single Pot Still
description: Ireland's own invention: a mash of malted and unmalted barley run through copper pots, yielding a creamy texture with a signature peppery spice. Found nowhere else on Earth.
funFact: The style's defining unmalted barley was originally added to sidestep a British tax on malted grain introduced in 1785.

name: Poitín
description: Ireland's legendary illicit spirit, once distilled in hidden hillside stills from barley, potatoes, or whatever the farm could spare. Fierce, unaged, and wrapped in three centuries of outlaw folklore.
funFact: Poitín was outlawed in Ireland in 1661 and its sale was not made legal again until 1997 — a prohibition lasting more than three centuries.

name: Advocaat
description: A thick, custard-like Dutch liqueur of egg yolks, sugar, and brandy spirit, eaten with a spoon as often as it is sipped. Winter's coziest curiosity.
funFact: The name likely traces to the avocado drinks Dutch colonists encountered in the Americas; back home, egg yolks stood in for the unavailable fruit.

name: Allspice Dram
description: A rum-based Jamaican liqueur steeped with allspice berries, tasting of the whole spice rack at once. A tiny pour warms tiki drinks like a crackling fire.
funFact: Allspice got its English name because the berry seems to combine the flavors of cinnamon, nutmeg, and clove in a single spice.

name: Amaretto
description: Italy's marzipan-scented charmer, whose name means 'little bitter.' It radiates almond sweetness in sours, coffee, and desserts alike.
funFact: Many amarettos, including the famous Disaronno, get their almond-like flavor not from almonds at all but from apricot kernels.

name: Blue Curaçao
description: Orange curaçao in a flamboyant azure costume. The flavor is pure orange; the electric color is pure showmanship, beloved by tropical drinks everywhere.
funFact: Blue curaçao tastes essentially identical to its orange sibling; the famous color comes purely from added food dye.

name: Coffee Liqueur
description: Dark roast energy in liqueur form, sweet and bittersweet at once. It naps inside White Russians by day and fuels espresso martinis by night.
funFact: Kahlúa, the world's best-known coffee liqueur, launched in 1936 and is made with arabica coffee grown in the Mexican state of Veracruz.

name: Crème de Cassis
description: A deep purple blackcurrant liqueur from Burgundy, jammy and tart in equal measure. A splash transforms white wine into a kir and champagne into a kir royale.
funFact: The kir cocktail is named after Canon Félix Kir, a World War II resistance figure and mayor of Dijon who tirelessly served the drink to visiting dignitaries.

name: Crème de Menthe
description: Liquid after-dinner mint, appearing in both emerald and colorless forms. It freshens grasshoppers and stingers with a cool peppermint breeze.
funFact: The 'crème' in crème de menthe refers to the liqueur's high sugar content and syrupy texture; it contains no cream at all.

name: Crème de Violette
description: A purple liqueur that tastes the way violets smell, painting cocktails the color of dusk. It gives the Aviation its famous sky-at-twilight hue.
funFact: Crème de violette all but vanished from American shelves for decades until it was reintroduced in 2007, rescuing the Aviation cocktail from extinction.

name: Elderflower Liqueur
description: A perfumed nectar of tiny white elderflower blossoms, sweet and springlike. It slips gracefully into everything from spritzes to martinis, improving nearly all of them.
funFact: St-Germain, the brand that launched the modern elderflower craze in 2007, became so ubiquitous in cocktails that bartenders nicknamed it 'bartender's ketchup.'

name: Falernum
description: Barbados' spiced secret weapon: a low-proof liqueur of lime, ginger, clove, and almond. A few dashes and any rum drink suddenly sounds like a steel drum band.
funFact: Falernum's name may derive from Falernian wine, the most celebrated wine of ancient Rome, and it also exists as a non-alcoholic syrup.

name: Irish Cream
description: A silky truce between Irish whiskey and fresh dairy cream, with chocolate playing peacemaker. It appears wherever coffee, dessert, or holidays are found.
funFact: When Baileys was being invented in the early 1970s, its creators fixed the harsh-tasting first whiskey-and-cream prototype by stirring in powdered drinking chocolate.

name: Limoncello
description: Bottled Amalfi sunshine, made by steeping lemon zest in spirit until it glows. Served glacially cold after dinner, it is Italy's brightest digestivo.
funFact: Traditional limoncello uses only the fragrant zest of the lemons, never the juice, which is why it is sweet and aromatic rather than sour.

name: Maraschino Liqueur
description: A crystal-clear cherry liqueur distilled from marasca cherries, pits and all, giving it a funky almond-and-flowers mystique. The secret handshake of classic cocktails like the Last Word.
funFact: The Luxardo family made maraschino in Zadar for over a century before rebuilding in Italy after World War II, replanting their marasca cherry orchards from scratch.

name: Nocino
description: An inky Italian liqueur brewed from unripe green walnuts, bittersweet and mysterious. Farmhouse alchemy passed down through Emilian families for generations.
funFact: Tradition dictates that the green walnuts for nocino be harvested on St. John's Eve, June 23rd to 24th, while they are still soft enough to cut.

name: Orange Curaçao
description: A richer, often brandy-based cousin of triple sec born of the Caribbean's most stubborn orange. Its deep candied-peel warmth is a tiki and classic-cocktail essential.
funFact: Curaçao is flavored with the laraha, a bitter orange that evolved from Valencia orange trees the Spanish planted on the island, which turned inedible in the arid soil.

name: Peach Schnapps
description: A sweet, sunny peach liqueur that ruled 1980s American bars. Unashamedly fun, it still powers the fuzzy navel and sex on the beach.
funFact: American 'schnapps' is a sweet liqueur, unlike traditional German and Austrian schnaps, which is an unsweetened fruit distillate.

name: Triple Sec
description: The tireless workhorse of the orange liqueur clan, clear and citrus-bright. It quietly powers margaritas, cosmopolitans, and sidecars around the globe.
funFact: No one is entirely sure what the 'triple' in triple sec originally meant; even the historic French producers tell conflicting stories about it.

name: Umeshu
description: A Japanese liqueur of whole ume fruit steeped in spirit and sugar, balancing honeyed sweetness with almond-tinged tartness. Often homemade and aged like a family heirloom.
funFact: The ume used in umeshu is usually translated as 'plum,' but the fruit is botanically closer to an apricot.

name: Clairin
description: Haiti's untamed cane spirit, fermented with wild yeasts and distilled by hundreds of small village stills. No two batches are quite alike, like encountering a shiny variant every time.
funFact: Haiti is home to an estimated 500-plus small clairin distilleries, most using wild fermentation and local heirloom sugarcane varieties.

name: Dark Rum
description: A brooding, molasses-rich creature that lurks at the bottom of tiki drinks and floats ominously on top of them. Deep aging and dark molasses give it heavyweight flavor.
funFact: Goslings trademarked the Dark 'n' Stormy cocktail, so by the letter of the trademark an authentic one must be made with Goslings Black Seal rum.

name: Demerara Rum
description: A dark, smoky-sweet rum from the banks of Guyana's Demerara River. Its burnt-sugar depth is the secret engine of classic tiki recipes.
funFact: Guyana's Diamond Distillery still operates the world's last working wooden Coffey still, along with heritage wooden pot stills that are centuries-old designs.

name: Gold Rum
description: White rum's sun-kissed evolution, mellowed by time in oak barrels. Rounder and warmer, it bridges the gap between mixable lightness and sipping depth.
funFact: The golden color comes from barrel aging, though many producers also adjust the hue with a small amount of caramel coloring.

name: Jamaican Pot Still Rum
description: The funkiest member of the rum family, famed for its intense fruity 'hogo.' Long wild fermentations and pot stills breed esters that smell like overripe pineapple and banana.
funFact: Some Jamaican distilleries boost esters using 'muck pits,' aged reservoirs of leftover fermentation material that supercharge the rum's signature funk.

name: Overproof Rum
description: The fire-breathing form of rum, bottled well above standard strength. Handle with respect: it powers flaming tiki garnishes and adds a roaring backbone to punches.
funFact: The word 'proof' comes from an old test in which spirit was mixed with gunpowder; if the powder still ignited, the rum was 'proved' strong enough.

name: Rhum Agricole
description: A grassy, wild-hearted rum distilled from fresh-pressed sugarcane juice instead of molasses. It tastes like a cane field after rain and stars in the Ti' Punch.
funFact: Rhum agricole from Martinique earned a French AOC designation in 1996, a protection more commonly associated with wine and cheese than with spirits.

name: Spiced Rum
description: A rum that raided the spice cabinet and never looked back. Vanilla, cinnamon, and clove cling to a sweet cane base, making it the gateway species for many trainers.
funFact: Captain Morgan is named after Henry Morgan, a real 17th-century Welsh privateer who later became lieutenant governor of Jamaica.

name: White Rum
description: The clear, quick-footed starter of the rum family, filtered to a clean gleam. It hides in plain sight inside daiquiris and mojitos, striking with soft sugarcane sweetness.
funFact: Bacardí's bat logo comes from the fruit bats that roosted in the company's first distillery, which Doña Amalia Bacardí considered a sign of good luck.

name: Blended Malt Scotch
description: A marriage of single malts from multiple distilleries with no grain whisky invited. All the malt character, none of the single-distillery ego.
funFact: This style was known as 'vatted malt' until the Scotch Whisky Regulations of 2009 officially renamed it 'blended malt.'

name: Blended Scotch
description: Malt whisky's charisma married to grain whisky's smoothness, assembled by master blenders chasing perfect consistency. The workhorse that carried Scotch around the globe.
funFact: Blends account for roughly 90% of all Scotch whisky sold worldwide, dwarfing the single malts that get most of the glory.

name: Campbeltown Single Malt
description: Briny, oily, faintly funky malts from a tiny peninsula town that whisky history nearly forgot. What survived is fiercely loved and stubbornly old-fashioned.
funFact: Victorian-era Campbeltown called itself the whisky capital of the world with over 30 distilleries; today it remains a protected Scotch region with only three in operation.

name: Highland Single Malt
description: Malts from Scotland's biggest and most varied region, ranging from heathery and floral to muscular and faintly smoky. A region so large it refuses to have one personality.
funFact: The Highlands are geographically the largest of Scotland's legally protected whisky regions, stretching from just north of Glasgow to the far northern coast.

name: Island Single Malt
description: Maritime malts from Skye, Orkney, Jura, Arran, and Mull — salt-licked, honeyed, and often kissed with smoke. Each island argues, convincingly, that it tastes like nowhere else.
funFact: The Islands are not a legally recognized Scotch region — under the official rules, every island distillery except those on Islay is classified as Highland.

name: Islay Single Malt
description: The smoke-breathing dragon of Scotch: peat-fired malts from a windswept Hebridean island, tasting of bonfires, sea spray, and old rope. You never forget your first.
funFact: Islay is home to around ten working distilleries despite having a population of only about 3,000 people.

name: Lowland Single Malt
description: Light, grassy, and gently floral malts from Scotland's southern belt, historically triple-distilled into silkiness. The aperitif of the Scotch family.
funFact: Lowland malts were historically nicknamed the 'Lowland Ladies' for their delicate character, and some distilleries there still practice traditional triple distillation.

name: Single Grain Scotch
description: Column-distilled whisky from one distillery using grains beyond malted barley — light, sweet, and long the unseen backbone of every great blend. Increasingly bottled on its own for the curious.
funFact: The 'single' refers to a single distillery, not a single grain — a single grain Scotch can be made from several cereals at once.

name: Speyside Single Malt
description: Elegant, fruity malts from the valley of the River Spey, where distilleries cluster thicker than anywhere else on Earth. The honeyed diplomat of the Scotch world.
funFact: Speyside packs roughly 50 distilleries into one small river valley, the densest concentration of whisky-making on the planet.

name: Grain Vodka
description: The stealth specialist of the spirits world, distilled from wheat, rye, or corn to near-silence. Its subtle texture and faint grain sweetness carry countless cocktails without a sound.
funFact: US regulations long defined vodka as being 'without distinctive character, aroma, taste, or color,' wording the TTB finally removed in 2020.

name: Potato Vodka
description: A fuller-bodied, earthier vodka variant with a creamy weight on the tongue. Despite the stereotype, it is the rarer breed, as potatoes are stubborn to distill.
funFact: Only a small fraction of the world's vodka is actually made from potatoes; they are bulkier, starchier, and more expensive to process than grain.

name: Aquavit
description: Scandinavia's caraway-and-dill spirit, sipped ice-cold at feasts with a hearty skål. It tastes like rye bread's spirited ghost.
funFact: Norwegian 'linie' aquavit is aged in sherry casks aboard ships that cross the equator twice, a sea voyage the makers credit with mellowing the spirit.

name: Awamori
description: Okinawa's ancestral rice spirit, fermented with black koji and long-grain Thai rice, sometimes aged for decades in clay pots. Japan's oldest distilled spirit, with island soul.
funFact: Awamori is considered Japan's oldest distilled spirit, born of 15th-century trade between the Ryukyu Kingdom and Siam, which is why it still uses Thai indica rice.

name: Baijiu
description: China's ancient grain spirit, fermented solid-state in earthen pits with a microbial culture called qu. Ferociously aromatic and nearly mythical to Western drinkers.
funFact: Baijiu is the best-selling spirit category on Earth by volume, yet the overwhelming majority of it is consumed within China.

name: Feni
description: Goa's pungent double-distilled spirit made from cashew apples or coconut palm sap. Wildly aromatic, farmhouse-funky, and fiercely protected as an Indian heritage drink.
funFact: Cashew feni received a Geographical Indication in 2009, making it one of the first Indian spirits legally tied to its home state of Goa.

name: Shochu
description: Japan's versatile, gently savory spirit, single-distilled from sweet potato, barley, rice, or buckwheat with the help of koji mold. Subtle where baijiu is loud.
funFact: In 2003, shochu shipments overtook sake within Japan, a milestone in the homeland of both drinks.

name: Soju
description: Korea's smooth, lightly sweet spirit in its iconic green bottle. Easygoing yet relentless, it accompanies Korean barbecue the way rain accompanies clouds.
funFact: Jinro soju has repeatedly ranked as the world's best-selling spirit brand by volume, outselling every famous vodka and whisky label.

name: Canadian Whisky
description: Light, smooth blends built grain by grain, where each cereal is often distilled and aged separately before assembly. Canadians call nearly all of it 'rye' out of sheer tradition.
funFact: Canadian rules famously allow up to one-eleventh (9.09%) of other aged spirits or wine to be blended into whisky destined for the U.S. market.

name: Indian Single Malt
description: Malt whisky matured at tropical speed, where the subcontinental heat does in four years what Scotland needs twelve to accomplish. Bold, jammy, and in a hurry.
funFact: India's hot climate can evaporate over 10% of a maturing cask per year — several times the 'angel's share' lost annually in Scotland.

name: Japanese Whisky
description: Scotch's meticulous Japanese apprentice that grew into a master: precise, balanced whiskies built for quiet contemplation or the perfect highball. Restraint as a flavor.
funFact: Masataka Taketsuru learned whisky-making in Scotland around 1919, helped build Japan's first whisky distillery for Suntory, then left to found its great rival, Nikka.

name: Taiwanese Single Malt
description: Subtropical single malt that ages at a sprint and drinks like a mango orchard met a sherry cask. The upstart that made the old world nervous.
funFact: Taiwan's Kavalan distillery only released its first whisky in 2008, yet by 2015 one of its casks was named the world's best single malt at the World Whiskies Awards.
